I'm raising this as an MS for Carmarthenshire, but I need to declare that I am also the Chair of the Local Government, Housing and Planning Committee. Trefnydd, can I ask for a statement from the Welsh Government on nutrient neutrality and its impact on housing delivery in west Wales?

Following Natural Resources Wales's marine assessment and subsequent planning advice to councils last year, social and affordable housing schemes across Carmarthenshire and Pembrokeshire face significant delays. I have been contacted by one contractor who builds almost exclusively for affordable social housing, and he has an order book of £30 million-worth of secured work that has now stalled. Its turnover has halved, it supports approximately 80 staff and 320 subcontractors, from groundworkers and bricklayers through to merchants, plant hire firms and delivery drivers. Everyone accepts in this Chamber the need to protect our rivers and estuaries, but nutrient pollution comes from a wide range of sources across whole catchment areas. These delays are affecting both families waiting for homes and the firms ready to build them.

So, can we have a statement on what has replaced the marine nitrates development taskforce, what further mitigation measures are being considered, and when these housing schemes can realistically move forward? Thank you.

contributions.text_english:
Trefnydd, as vice-chair of the executive committee for the Urdd Eisteddfod in Bro'r Wenynen, I'm pleased to say that holding the Urdd Eisteddfod in Newport next year will be an important and historic moment for our area. It's an opportunity not only to welcome thousands of visitors, but also to introduce more families, young people and children to the Welsh language and our national culture.

On Saturday, the welcome festival will take place in the centre of Newport, and everyone is welcome to join us at the celebration. For me, the important thing will be the legacy left by the Eisteddfod. Can I therefore ask for a statement describing how the Government will work with the Urdd, local authorities, schools and community groups to ensure that the Eisteddfod has a permanent impact on the use of the Welsh language, and on confidence in terms of community use across Casnewydd Islwyn, and Bro'r Wenynen in its entirety?
contributions.text_original:
Drefnydd, fel is-gadeirydd pwyllgor gwaith Eisteddfod yr Urdd Bro'r Wenynen, dwi'n falch o ddweud y bydd cynnal Eisteddfod yr Urdd yng Nghasnewydd y flwyddyn nesaf yn foment bwysig a hanesyddol iawn i'n hardal. Mae'n gyfle nid yn unig i groesawu miloedd o ymwelwyr, ond hefyd i gyflwyno mwy o blant, pobl ifanc a theuluoedd i'r Gymraeg a'n diwylliant cenedlaethol. 

Ddydd Sadwrn, bydd yr ŵyl groeso yn digwydd yng nghanol Casnewydd, ac mae croeso mawr i bawb fod yno i ddathlu. I mi, y peth pwysig fydd y gwaddol fydd yr Eisteddfod yn ei adael ar ei hôl. A gaf i felly ddatganiad, os gwelwch yn dda, sy'n disgrifio sut y bydd y Llywodraeth yn cydweithio â'r Urdd, awdurdodau lleol, ysgolion a grwpiau cymunedol i sicrhau bod yr Eisteddfod yn cael effaith barhaol ar y defnydd o'r Gymraeg, ac ar hyder defnydd cymunedol ledled Casnewydd Islwyn, a Bro'r Wenynen yn ei chyfanrwydd?

contributions.text_english:
I thank the Member, and good luck to everyone who is involved in that welcome festival. And I look forward to attending Eisteddfod Bro'r Wenynen next year. As the Member has said, it will be an excellent opportunity for the area. And we know of the boost that comes to an area and its Welshness when Eisteddfod yr Urdd goes to that area. 

Certainly, one of the things that I felt very frustrated about as an opposition spokesperson was that there was not enough planning being done in terms of legacy. And the assurance I'd like to give the Member, and every other Member, is that I and the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language are having discussions at the moment about how to put that legacy framework in place in terms of the Urdd Eisteddfod and the National Eisteddfod, and you will have heard me speaking about other events across Wales. 

There is investment, of course, from this Government going into that, and ensuring that that legacy work does not just fall on the very busy people who are currently fundraising for these eisteddfods, but that we can work with people such as the mentrau iaith on the ground to ensure that legacy, is very important. So, as that work continues, I will be very ready to share that with Members, and to take your ideas and input on board as well. Because these are important events. They do leave a legacy. But if we can have more of a legacy by planning more strategically, then that's where I and the Cabinet Minister for Welsh education want to reach.

Mi fydd o, fel mae'r Aelod wedi dweud, yn gyfle aruthrol i'r ardal. Ac rydyn ni'n gwybod yr hwb sy'n dod i ardal ac i Gymreictod pan fydd Eisteddfod yr Urdd yn dod yna. 

Yn sicr, mae o'n un o'r pethau roeddwn i'n teimlo'n rhwystredig iawn yn eu cylch, fel llefarydd yn yr wrthblaid, nad oedd digon o gynllunio yn cael ei wneud o ran gwaddol. A'r sicrwydd yr hoffwn i ei roi i'r Aelod, a phob Aelod arall, ydy fy mod innau a'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Addysg a'r Gymraeg yn cael trafodaethau ar y funud o ran sut mae rhoi'r fframwaith gwaddol yna yn ei le o ran Eisteddfod yr Urdd a'r Eisteddfod Genedlaethol, ac fe fyddwch wedi fy nghlywed yn sôn am ddigwyddiadau eraill ledled Cymru.

Mae yna fuddsoddiad, wrth gwrs, gan y Llywodraeth hon yn mynd i mewn i hynny, ac mae sicrhau bod y gwaith gwaddol hwnnw nid dim ond yn disgyn ar y bobl brysur iawn sydd yn codi arian tuag at yr eisteddfodau hyn, ond ein bod ni'n gallu gweithio efo rheini fel y mentrau iaith ar lawr gwlad i sicrhau gwaddol, yn eithriadol o bwysig. Felly, wrth i'r gwaith hwnnw fynd rhagddo, byddaf yn barod iawn i fod yn rhannu hwnnw gydag Aelodau, a chael eich mewnbwn a'ch syniadau chi hefyd. contributions.text_english: Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. I'd like to call for a statement from the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care on the increasing prevalence of antisemitism in the healthcare sector. The Campaign Against Antisemitism is today publishing a groundbreaking documentary featuring patients and practitioners describing experiences, including Nazi salutes, antisemitic death threats and patients refusing treatment from Jewish doctors. There has been a meteoric increase in antisemitism over the last three years, and British Jews have been taking steps to conceal their Jewish identity. Whilst most evidence focuses on England, I'd be surprised if Wales were immune from this problem. So, can we have a statement outlining how the Welsh Government is monitoring antisemitism in our healthcare services, and what action is being taken to root it out?

Whilst most evidence focuses on England, I'd be surprised if Wales were immune from this problem. So, can we have a statement outlining how the Welsh Government is monitoring antisemitism in our healthcare services, and what action is being taken to root it out?

contributions.text_english: Thank you. Can I be very clear that antisemitism is something that we should all condemn? We should all work proactively to ensure that no-one is targeted in such a way and feels unsafe. The growth of antisemitism and hatred is something that should unite all of us in condemning and working hard within our communities to ensure that there is community cohesion and that nobody is targeted in such a way. The Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality leads on this work on behalf of the Welsh Government, though it's of course owned collectively by each of us, and the 'Anti-racist Wales Action Plan' is being reviewed to ensure that it's fit for purpose in light of the rise that we're seeing in antisemitism and hate crimes. Therefore, any Member here who is concerned about such issues, please engage with this work, because it's crucial that we work together.

contributions.text_english: Trefnydd, I would like a statement from the relevant Minister on the criteria used in allocating additional funding to support people living in poverty. A press release last week on emergency food and poverty support noted that funding would not be allocated on the basis of the number of people living in poverty, but, rather, that an additional percentage of the funding will be distributed according to how rural a community is.
contributions.text_original: Drefnydd, hoffwn i gael datganiad gan y Gweinidog perthnasol ynghylch y meini prawf a ddefnyddir wrth ddyrannu cyllid ychwanegol i gefnogi pobl sy'n byw mewn tlodi. Nododd cyhoeddiad i'r wasg yr wythnos diwethaf ynghylch cymorth bwyd a thlodi brys na fydd cyllid yn cael ei ddyrannu ar sail nifer y bobl sy'n byw mewn tlodi, ond, yn hytrach, y bydd cyfran ychwanegol o'r cyllid yn cael ei ddosbarthu yn ôl pa mor wledig yw cymuned.

contributions.text_english: There's a long-established formula for the distribution of such funding, and well-established processes for making changes to this formula. Your Government has torn that up via a press release, and I'm told councils are still waiting for details nearly a week after the announcement was made. I find it deeply concerning, without debate or scrutiny, that the Plaid Government would divert potential funding away from communities such as Ely, Caerau, south Riverside, Pentrebane, Grangetown, Butetown and Splott, despite the significant challenges of poverty faced by residents there. Surely there's consensus across this Chamber that the most effective way to target funding intended to alleviate poverty is to allocate it according to the levels of poverty and need. The Minister needs to urgently explain why she believes differently. Diolch yn fawr.

Thank you. So the Member will be aware, the Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality is the relevant Member; you asked at the start of your question who the relevant Minister was, so just to give you that assurance.

Could I make it clear? It has been unequivocal in terms of this Government that tackling poverty in all parts of Wales is a priority for us. Or entire programme for government, if you look at it, that cross-Government focus, in every portfolio, is entirely clear that tackling poverty is incredibly important and is something that we prioritise. The Member will also be aware, I'm sure, that there are problems in terms of rural poverty in particular that need to be tackled. Often, that has been something that has been hidden, and it's very important that the support that we provide in order to ensure that everyone, in all corners of Wales—. We know that, in every constituency, there are people living in poverty who should not be living in poverty, and that the last Labour Government's record was to increase the number of children living in poverty. That is why it is a priority for this Government to work across Ministers to get to the heart of the problem.

contributions.text_english: We'll move on to our next item, a statement by the First Minister, 'New Ambition for Wales: Programme for Government 2026-2030'. I call on the First Minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth.
contributions.text_original: Symudwn ymlaen i'r eitem nesaf, datganiad gan y Prif Weinidog, 'Uchelgais Newydd i Gymru: Rhaglen Lywodraethu 2026-2030'. Galwaf ar y Prif Weinidog, Rhun ap Iorwerth.

contributions.text_english:
In May, the people of Wales said clearly that they wanted a new level of ambition for our nation. Acting on the mandate to set our sights higher than previous Governments have done and forge a more hopeful future for Wales, I am today proud to publish our programme for government. 'New Ambition for Wales' builds on the foundations established during the Government’s first 100 days and sets out how we will deliver the priorities identified in our manifesto over the Senedd term.

This programme is built around the issues that matter most to people’s everyday lives: the sustainability of the health and care service; the cost of living; high-skilled, well-paid jobs; driving up standards in education; tackling child poverty and opening doors for young people; and standing up for Wales at every turn.

'New Ambition for Wales' builds on the foundations established during the Government’s first 100 days and sets out how we will deliver the priorities identified in our manifesto over the Senedd term.

This programme is built around the issues that matter most to people’s everyday lives: the sustainability of the health and care service; the cost of living; high-skilled, well-paid jobs; driving up standards in education; tackling child poverty and opening doors for young people; and standing up for Wales at every turn.

contributions.text_english: For too long, the Welsh Government has been measured on the number of actions it takes and not the outcomes it delivers. That changes now. From now on, every action will have a clear purpose, namely to improve people’s lives. Prioritisation will be central to our approach. Effective government means focusing our efforts and resources on the areas where they can have the greatest impact, being clear about the outcomes that we want to achieve and being accountable for delivering them. That must always be the case, but it’s especially true at a time like this when resource is limited.

O hyn ymlaen, mi fydd gan bob cam gweithredu bwrpas clir, sef gwella bywydau pobl. Mi fydd blaenoriaethu yn ganolog i'n dull gweithredu. Mae llywodraeth effeithiol yn golygu canolbwyntio ein hymdrechion a'n hadnoddau ar y meysydd lle gallan nhw wneud y gwahaniaeth mwyaf, bod yn glir ynghylch y canlyniadau rydyn ni am eu sicrhau, a bod yn atebol am eu cyflawni nhw. Mi ddylai hynny fod yn wir bob amser, ond mae'n bwysicach nag erioed ar adeg pan fo adnoddau'n brin.

contributions.text_english: Dirprwy Lywydd, for too long, silo working has stood in the way of progress. This new Government will work across traditional boundaries to address the greatest challenges facing our society. That is why prevention, productivity, the climate and nature emergency and the Welsh Language—Cymraeg—are embedded throughout every aspect of our programme. They are not separate priorities, they underpin every aspect of how we will deliver change and improve outcomes across Wales. They will shape the work of every Minister and every part of Government.

contributions.text_english:
At its heart, the aim of this programme is building a better future for Wales. Guided by the principles of the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015, we have brought together our well-being objectives and our programme for government into one single framework—a framework that sets out the future that we want to build and the actions that we will take to deliver it.

So, what does this mean in practice? It means prioritising the areas where we can have the greatest impact. A health and care service that is fit for the future is something that every Welsh citizen needs and deserves. This not only means taking immediate action to bring down waiting lists, which remain unacceptably high, but also ensuring that our most precious public service is sustainable and resilient for the future.

Yn ei hanfod, nod y rhaglen yma ydy creu dyfodol gwell i Gymru. Gan ddilyn egwyddorion Deddf Llesiant Cenedlaethau’r Dyfodol (Cymru) 2015, rydym ni wedi dod â'n hamcanion llesiant a'n rhaglen lywodraethu ynghyd mewn un fframwaith—fframwaith sy'n nodi'r dyfodol rydyn ni am ei greu a'r camau fyddwn ni'n eu cymryd i gyflawni hynny.

Felly, beth mae hyn yn ei olygu'n ymarferol? Mae'n golygu blaenoriaethu'r meysydd lle gallwn ni gael yr effaith fwyaf. Mae gwasanaeth iechyd a gofal sy'n ffit ar gyfer y dyfodol yn rhywbeth y mae pob dinesydd Cymreig ei angen ac yn ei haeddu. Mae hyn nid yn unig yn golygu cymryd camau ar unwaith i leihau'r rhestrau aros sy'n parhau'n annerbyniol o hir, ond hefyd sicrhau bod ein gwasanaethau cyhoeddus mwyaf gwerthfawr yn gynaliadwy ac yn wydn ar gyfer y dyfodol.

contributions.text_english:
We'll rebalance resources towards the prevention of ill health, better access to services and improved social care. We want a future where preventing ill health is given the same priority as treating illness, where services are designed around people and communities, and where every part of Government works together to improve health and well-being. And as the cost-of-living crisis continues to bite and global headwinds threaten further volatility in coming months, my Government will help households make ends meet.

At a time when many families are facing significant financial pressures, we will take action to make everyday life more affordable. Central to that effort is our transformative new childcare offer, which will help families with the cost of living, support parents into work and training and make a significant contribution to tackling child poverty. We will also tackle one of the biggest pressures on household budgets by improving access to affordable and secure housing, including through our commitment to deliver at least 20,000 additional social homes by 2030.

contributions.text_english: Last week, my colleague the Cabinet Minister for Finance announced a 30 per cent cut to business rates for the leisure and hospitality sectors. This decision was widely welcomed by the industry, and it reflects this Government's determination to give people practical support in challenging times. This, of course, is inherently linked to our aim to unleash the potential of Wales's economy and to create high-skilled jobs that pay well.

Mae'r penderfyniad yma wedi cael ei groesawu yn eang gan y diwydiant, ac mae e'n adlewyrchu ymrwymiad y Llywodraeth hon i roi cymorth ymarferol i bobl ar adegau heriol. contributions.text_english:
Our ambition for Wales rests on a flourishing economy that fuels our public services, creates fulfilling and rewarding jobs, and provides the foundation for a stronger future. Through our productivity mission, we'll work to halve the productivity gap with the rest of the UK within 10 years. We'll also establish a new national development agency to help Welsh businesses to grow, innovate and create good jobs. Every part of the Government has a role to play in growing the Welsh economy.

Dirprwy Lywydd, every child and young person deserves the opportunity to fulfil their potential and succeed in the future. But they've been failed by previous administrations whose lack of ambition has left Wales languishing at the bottom of league tables.

Prif Weinidog, can I begin by thanking you for delivering your programme for government today? There's plenty in this programme that Reform can agree with. We want waiting lists down, we want standards in our schools to improve, we want better paid jobs, stronger businesses, and a health service that people can access when they need it. Where there is common ground, I will say so.

Reform went into the election supporting greater surgical and diagnostic capacity, stronger literacy and numeracy in schools, reform of the additional learning needs system, more vocational opportunities for young people and a stronger future for family farms up and down the country. But the real test of this programme is not how many promises are made today, it's whether we can come back to this Chamber in a year, two years and four years from now and measure whether anything has actually improved.

contributions.text_english:
Holding you to account is our responsibility as an effective opposition. Take the NHS. You're promising up to 10 surgical hubs, more diagnostic capacity, stronger clinical pathways and up to 100 more general practitioners. Those are ambitious commitments and people will expect this Government to deliver them. So, my first question is this: by the end of this Senedd term, how much lower should the overall waiting lists be, when will those surgical hubs be operating at full capacity and how many additional patients will they treat? Give us the baseline. Give us the target. Give us the date. Then, this Senedd can hold you to it. 

The same applies to education. Your programme says that raising literacy and numeracy is one of the most urgent challenges facing our schools. I would agree. It also accepts the problems around persistent absence, behaviour and the pressure on the additional learning needs system. I welcome the fact that the Government recognises those problems, but recognition is the easy part. Schools cannot employ additional support with warm words, and local authorities cannot satisfy the growing demand for support with another review.

So, my second question is this: what improvement in attendance, literacy and numeracy should we expect to see by 2030, and what additional resource will actually reach the schools and councils to make the ALN system sustainable? Again, put the numbers against it. Parents and teachers need to know what success looks like. We on these opposition benches need to know what your idea of success looks like.

There is a much clearer political difference between us on the economy. This Government wants new agencies, commissions and programmes. Reform went into the election offering a different approach. We want lower taxes, better roads, stronger infrastructure and a Government that makes it easier for businesses to invest and grow here in Cymru. Your programme talks about productivity and good jobs. Fine. Productivity can be measured. Pay can be measured. Economic inactivity can be measured. Business creation can be measured. So, my third question is this: which economic measure does the First Minister want us to judge him by in 2030, and what target is he setting himself? Because if the answer is that Wales will be more prosperous, that is not enough. We need to know what progress looks like in hard figures.

I will now move on to the areas on which Reform fundamentally disagrees. First Minister, your Government remains committed to a pathway to net zero by 2040. Reform does not support that devolved target. We put greater weight on affordability, energy security and nuclear power, including the economic opportunity through small modular reactors at Wylfa in north Wales, which did not feature at all in Plaid Cymru's election manifesto. In fact, there's not much talk of north Wales at all in your programme for government, which is extremely disappointing.

On farming, you intend to continue and refine the sustainable farming scheme. We campaigned for much more substantial reform, with food production taking precedence and bureaucracy taking a back seat, rather than form filling and farming by calendar, which risks driving livestock numbers down in Wales. Those are fair and genuine differences, and people can judge the outcomes for themselves.

I also want to address the constitutional section of this programme, because it goes well beyond asking Westminster for a fair funding settlement. You are establishing a new national commission for Wales. You want justice and policing devolved, welfare devolved, further powers over energy, broadcasting, water and the Crown Estate. And Government is formally asking for the power to determine the timing, question and process of an independence referendum. Plaid Cymru is entitled to argue for those things. Reform is equally entitled to oppose them. I will never accept the notion that you have to support independence and constitutional chaos to prove you believe in Wales.

First Minister, I'm interested in what works, not what fits an ideology. Being Welsh does not require supporting independence, and standing up for Wales does not require wanting to leave the United Kingdom. So, my fourth question is this: how much public money and civil service resource will be committed to this constitutional programme during this Senedd term, and what practical outcome will you use to show that the expenditure has improved people's day-to-day lives?

Your own well-being statement says that the programme for government will be reviewed every year, and that progress will be reported annually. Good. And those reports must contain enough hard information for this Senedd and the public to judge whether you are delivering. By 2030, will people be waiting less time for treatment? Will children be attending school more regularly and achieving better results? Will wages and productivity be higher? Will businesses have confidence and invest in Wales? Will Welsh farmers be unshackled from burdensome red tape and incentivised to increase food production? I'm asking you to tell us what success looks like in numbers and time frames. Set the measures now, publish them every year, and then we will see whether this Government delivers what it has promised. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english:
I'm grateful to the leader of Reform for agreeing that we are getting our priorities right in this programme for government and pledging to work in a co-operative way to help us deliver. That's exactly how I think we should operate here.

The Member is quite right that we need a Government that is willing and wants to be held to account. Scrutiny is important. That is why we have already published the first iteration of our digital dashboard. It will develop, it will grow, enabling you, and the Welsh public, to see how we are performing against a range of targets. Yes, and of course we have elements of targets throughout our programme for government.

There are some things that we have done already. We don't need a target to say that we will deliver that £1 billion that shows Welsh agriculture that this is a Government that believes in them and wants to support them. These are actions already taken. We don't need to set a target for how much funding we think needs to go into the health service. We've already taken those actions.

But the Member is quite right, so let's have a look at a number of the really key targets. We couldn't be clearer about what the childcare offer means. We have already been able to get to a point where the outcome at the end of this financial year is the roll-out of 12.5 hours of funded childcare for every two-year-old in every part of Wales. That's something the previous administration singularly failed to do. They got up to three. We're getting up to 22.

On education, interestingly, the work that we need to do—you have a background in education—is find a baseline from which we then are able to build. There will be targets around elements such as the Programme for International Student Assessment, which is only one measure, but we absolutely are putting those baselines in place so that we can build exactly that framework around which schools and parents and pupils know what they're aiming for.

There's a question about productivity. What are our targets on productivity? The Cabinet Minister for enterprise has literally published the first proper target for economic growth in Wales for a quarter of a century. It’s pretty ambitious, but I know that we have got the means to get there. It is, as it happens, not within the life of this Senedd, because we have to think long term about the economy. This is halving the productivity gap with the rest of the UK within 10 years. Now, that is a significant target, and throughout the term of this Senedd and beyond, as a nation, we need to be working towards those kinds of ambitious targets.

So, the targets are there. The differences that the Member emphasised are ones that are clear for everybody to see: that Reform do not believe in Wales as a nation, that we are a nation that builds our own future. That is my belief. I believed in devolution in 1997, when we had the chance to vote. I believed in strengthening it when we had the referendum in 2011. I believe we need to strengthen it further. What we have from the leader of Reform is a blanket ‘no’: ‘We do not want Wales to have the tools. We do not want Wales to be able to succeed by having the powers or the finances in order to build a better future for Wales.’ That is fine, that is a fundamental difference between us. I'll be the one here standing up for Wales. She can do as she pleases.

contributions.text_english:
First Minister, can I also thank you for your statement today and congratulate you on publishing your programme for government? This, of course, is the first non-Welsh Labour-led programme for government this Senedd has seen, and we aim to respond to it in a dignified manner, putting the people that we serve and represent first, and of course working in common cause where and when we can. I look forward to working constructively on legislation in particular.

Now, governing, as I believe you recognise, is hard, and we do not intend to make your task unnecessarily harder, but we do represent in our party a great Welsh tradition with deep bonds of solidarity across Britain on the basis that we achieve more together than we can achieve alone. And our role in this Chamber is to stand up for the most vulnerable and to be a voice for those who don't have inherited wealth and privilege, but who graft and work for a better tomorrow. We were therefore disappointed that one of the first things this Plaid Cymru Government did was to water down its offer on free school meals. Plaid Cymru promised in its first 100 days document to commit to expanding free school meals to all secondary school pupils in households claiming universal benefit from September of this year. But by June, of course, just weeks after the election, you stated that this year it would only be available to parents of children in years 7 and 8. No date, indeed, has been given for extending this to years 9, 10 and 11.

Now, Bevan said that socialism is the language of priorities, and one of your first decisions was that you decided that keeping an election promise to some of our poorest children was not a priority. When over £300 million of ALN consequentials came to Wales, again you decided that the most vulnerable children were not a priority and not a penny was allocated to them. Welsh Labour had published plans in Government and in our manifesto for a negotiating body for school support staff, and despite the Senedd voting in favour of it, your Government has refused to commit to supporting school support staff on this.

Now, First Minister, you told traditional Labour voters in your election campaign that you were a safe pair of hands for progressive voters, and yet your group is now welcoming right-wing Reformers. And in your first decisions on education and opportunity for everyone, you've prioritised expanding Welsh Labour's childcare offer to millionaires. First Minister, can I ask you today to commit that your policies in this programme for government will not result in the removal or reduction in support aimed at working class or vulnerable children, such as Flying Start?

Turning to healthcare, under this Plaid Cymru Government, both overall waiting lists and two-year waiting lists are rising again, having fallen for 10 months in a row under Welsh Labour. Before the election, you promised that, within months, the number of people waiting for more than two years would be zero. Can you confirm that the priorities that you set out in this programme for government will not see you renege on another promise—a promise, not just an ambition, that we will see two-year waits reduced to zero within months? And can you confirm how many months that will be?

Weeks before the election—in an attempt, obviously, to get Wales's trade union movement on side—you also wrote to Cwm Taf health visitors supporting their call to upgrade all band 6 health visitors to band 7. Ministers, again, have reneged on this promise, and health visitors rightly feel betrayed. So, can I ask you, First Minister, will you now make good on your promise to these workers and to Unite the Union?

Others who will feel ignored and betrayed by this programme for government are the people of north Wales, as Helen Jenner has already identified, specifically those in Flintshire and Wrexham, because as Wrexham.com have observed, for north-east Wales, a notable feature is absence. It's as though parts of Wales are already being left behind. Standing up for Wales means uniting the people of Wales, not seeking a course of action that will divide Wales, divide the nation, divide our families and divide our communities, as Brexit did. Standing up for Wales means taking action to improve Wales, not producing a plethora of plans.

It's not too late, though. It's not too late. I ask you, finally, First Minister, to work with us in the spirit that you campaigned, in the spirit not only of constructive politics, but also progressive politics, because when the people of Wales are prioritised, I can assure you that you will find in us a willing and constructive partner.

First Minister, can I also thank you for your statement today and congratulate you on publishing your programme for government? This, of course, is the first non-Welsh Labour-led programme for government this Senedd has seen, and we aim to respond to it in a dignified manner, putting the people that we serve and represent first, and of course working in common cause where and when we can. I look forward to working constructively on legislation in particular.

Now, governing, as I believe you recognise, is hard, and we do not intend to make your task unnecessarily harder, but we do represent in our party a great Welsh tradition with deep bonds of solidarity across Britain on the basis that we achieve more together than we can achieve alone. And our role in this Chamber is to stand up for the most vulnerable and to be a voice for those who don't have inherited wealth and privilege, but who graft and work for a better tomorrow. We were therefore disappointed that one of the first things this Plaid Cymru Government did was to water down its offer on free school meals. Plaid Cymru promised in its first 100 days document to commit to expanding free school meals to all secondary school pupils in households claiming universal benefit from September of this year. But by June, of course, just weeks after the election, you stated that this year it would only be available to parents of children in years 7 and 8. No date, indeed, has been given for extending this to years 9, 10 and 11.

Now, Bevan said that socialism is the language of priorities, and one of your first decisions was that you decided that keeping an election promise to some of our poorest children was not a priority. When over £300 million of ALN consequentials came to Wales, again you decided that the most vulnerable children were not a priority and not a penny was allocated to them. Welsh Labour had published plans in Government and in our manifesto for a negotiating body for school support staff, and despite the Senedd voting in favour of it, your Government has refused to commit to supporting school support staff on this.

Now, First Minister, you told traditional Labour voters in your election campaign that you were a safe pair of hands for progressive voters, and yet your group is now welcoming right-wing Reformers. And in your first decisions on education and opportunity for everyone, you've prioritised expanding Welsh Labour's childcare offer to millionaires. First Minister, can I ask you today to commit that your policies in this programme for government will not result in the removal or reduction in support aimed at working class or vulnerable children, such as Flying Start?

Turning to healthcare, under this Plaid Cymru Government, both overall waiting lists and two-year waiting lists are rising again, having fallen for 10 months in a row under Welsh Labour. Before the election, you promised that, within months, the number of people waiting for more than two years would be zero. Can you confirm that the priorities that you set out in this programme for government will not see you renege on another promise—a promise, not just an ambition, that we will see two-year waits reduced to zero within months? And can you confirm how many months that will be?

Weeks before the election—in an attempt, obviously, to get Wales's trade union movement on side—you also wrote to Cwm Taf health visitors supporting their call to upgrade all band 6 health visitors to band 7. Ministers, again, have reneged on this promise, and health visitors rightly feel betrayed. So, can I ask you, First Minister, will you now make good on your promise to these workers and to Unite the Union?

Others who will feel ignored and betrayed by this programme for government are the people of north Wales, as Helen Jenner has already identified, specifically those in Flintshire and Wrexham, because as Wrexham.com have observed, for north-east Wales, a notable feature is absence. It's as though parts of Wales are already being left behind. Standing up for Wales means uniting the people of Wales, not seeking a course of action that will divide Wales, divide the nation, divide our families and divide our communities, as Brexit did. Standing up for Wales means taking action to improve Wales, not producing a plethora of plans.

It's not too late, though. It's not too late. I ask you, finally, First Minister, to work with us in the spirit that you campaigned, in the spirit not only of constructive politics, but also progressive politics, because when the people of Wales are prioritised, I can assure you that you will find in us a willing and constructive partner.

contributions.text_english:
I thank the Labour leader for beginning his contribution in a positive way. Governing is hard, as he knows. There has never been a majority in the history of devolution, and we recognise that we need to work across this Chamber in many ways, including through the development of legislation, which he suggested he wants to work with us on.

Unpicking a bit more some of the points that were raised there—on the NHS, it was and is priority No. 1. This is a Government that has already made choices, including on a budget deal with the last Labour Government, to ensure that we have the resources to make sure that we build a more sustainable future for the NHS. We begin now from the point of the legacy that we inherited from the last Labour Government. Data is just coming through now from the time of the election and the weeks following that, and, yes, it confirms how dire the situation is that we are trying to resolve. But through the measures outlined in this programme for government, building towards the introduction of up to 10 hubs, a change in emphasis in terms of the work patterns of doctors—this is clinically led, remember, to free up time, to get more people through the system—the injection of £150 million, some of it clinical, some of it on the actual buildings themselves, which will be the home of a sustainable NHS for the future, we stand firm by the pledges that we have made and in making this a priority.

On this element of somehow north Wales not being mentioned in this programme for government, I come from even further north than he does, and this is a Government—and I have made it clear—that isn't about the tokenism of having a north Wales Minister; every single Minister in this Government is a north Wales Minister and a south Wales Minister and a west Wales Minister, because we believe in bringing Wales together and building a brighter future for people, wherever they are. And to attack the first north Wales First Minister for somehow not caring about the north isn't something that people are going to even believe makes sense, frankly.

I come back to additional learning needs and remind the Member again that he had £9 million that Labour were going to put into something that we consider to be very important; we're glad that he does too. We had £100 million on the table; we have £40 million that we can spend this year. That is what this party put on the table, seriously, in a way that isn't just money but is money that can be spent—money that can be spent to make a real difference to councils, to schools, to parents, to children. The offer is still very much available. This has to be about more than politics.

And I will end, if I may, on this attack, which I've heard mentioned and read about it in the paper—and I was thinking, 'Surely, he's not going to make this accusation here in the Senedd Chamber'—that the childcare offer is something that he objects to in its universality. So, suddenly, the Labour Party objects to the universality that provides bus passes for pensioners, so we can assume that Labour wants to take away bus passes for pensioners, we can assume that they're against the universality of free prescriptions. Can we start thinking that also they want the universality of the NHS, even, to be taken away from people? Is he happy to create a two-tier system where rich people are to be supported to go off into private healthcare, or does he, like me, believe that the more we can build together—yes, including that principle of universality—binds us together as a nation and gives us solutions for the long term that address the needs of people in all parts of Wales from all backgrounds?

We have here a programme for government that is about transforming Wales, and I guess the point to make on governing being difficult is that government is difficult, especially when you inherit a broad range of issues that don't put us off, that don't make us diminish our ambitions, but make us work harder to deliver them for the people of Wales.

It's always interesting watching a messy divorce—[Laughter.]—and, my goodness, has it been an untidy one.

Can I thank you, First Minister, for advance notice of your statement, although not quite as in advance as the Western Mail's notice of your statement today, which seemed to have more detail than any Member of this Senedd prior to the release of it at 9.34 a.m. this morning? I'm afraid to say, again, a bit of a sense of déjà vu, a lot of recutting and rehashing of your manifesto, recutting and rehashing of your 100-day plan, and there's only so much rehashing that you can do with the same sorry document so many times to try and polish what many people would describe as something that I won't refer to. Because that, I'm afraid, is what many people will see it as.

I have to say that I was listening carefully to the radio this morning, as you found out in First Minister's questions today, and Laura McAllister referred to your 100-day plan as a 'gimmick'—I agree with her, and it's not always that I agree with Laura McAllister, but I agree with her on that. And now, of course, the rubber needs to hit the road in terms of getting some delivery for the people of Wales. And it's not going very well so far, is it? Waiting times up, PISA scores down, your grandstanding on independence really not making much of a difference, no matter how loud you scream. Now, I will say that, look, there is a lot of ambition in this document that we on the Conservative benches share—we want to see a more prosperous Wales, we want to see a better educated Wales, we want to see a healthier Wales; we want to see all of those things—but I'm afraid that it's lighter on detail than I would like in terms of the availability to deliver on those things.

Let me just turn to the NHS for a second, because I'm very concerned about the NHS, as are you, and I know that it's something that is close to your heart. You referenced the climate emergency and the nature emergency; you didn't seem to reference a crisis in the NHS, which I'm afraid it is, and many people perceive it as such. One thing that we do know is that that crisis is largely caused, according to the clinicians themselves, and according to the royal colleges, including the Royal College of Nursing, which was here last week in the Senedd, as a result of the beds situation in our NHS. There simply aren't enough beds. The Labour Party was disastrous in terms of its management of the NHS; I agree with you on that. They cut the number of beds too far, too fast, and people now are paying the consequences.

Just over the last three years, I am told by the Royal College of Nursing, 21 per cent of acute surgical beds have gone in the Welsh NHS, a fifth of our capacity. Thirteen per cent of acute medical beds have gone. It's no wonder that our emergency departments can't find the beds in those hospitals when patients need them. You didn't reference that situation. I want to know what are you going to do to surge those beds in the short term to fix that issue. Because let me tell you: you create surgical hubs, you need beds for people to go into after they're recovering from surgery, particularly if something goes wrong. So, I want to know what are you doing on that front.

You also suggested that there's going to be a switch in the way that the NHS is funded, with more going to primary care. Now, I want more money to go into our primary care services, but I don't want it to be to the detriment of hospital care. What assurances can you give me today, First Minister, and the people of Wales, that you won't be cutting funding to our hospitals in Wales in order to compensate for that extra investment in primary care? Because we need to know.

You referenced the cost of living. I agree with you that we need action on that. That's why I raised the need to do something on council tax today in First Minister's questions. We need action to extend free childcare. We had a free childcare plan as well, and we'll support you to be able to try to deliver some more free childcare. Ours was slightly different; we wanted more parental choice so that grandparents could look after their children too, and that was better for the taxpayer in terms of cost. But I want to know what you're doing to cut taxes. Can you cut some taxes for us? A penny off income tax. Is it not possible to shave some money off the budget where we've got waste, where we've got largesse, so that we can put money back into people's pockets so that they can decide how to spend it in the economy themselves?

You referenced in your document—. By the way, when the statement came through, I clicked on the well-being link. It didn't work. I hope that's not an omen for the future in terms of whether you'll be able to deliver things. I eventually got around to finding the right link. You talked in there about the desire to allow people to buy their own community assets. I support that; we'll support you with that. I want people to be able to buy their own home. I want stamp duty gone. I want the right to buy back. I want to bring empty homes back into use. There's insufficient detail on those things in your plan.

I've got all sorts of other things that I'd like to discuss, but the clock's against me. Let me say this: if you're able to deliver on your ambitions, many of them which we support, we will try to work collaboratively with you. It might be difficult. There may be some stumbles along the way, but we're prepared to reach out on a cross-party basis, and it was good to hear the same message coming from Reform as well, to try to make Wales a better place. But be under no illusions: we want to see a Wales where there are lower taxes, where there's an end to wasteful spending, where there's less emphasis on the grandstanding and more emphasis on the day-to-day jobs and using those powers and resources that you already have in your armoury to deliver a better future for our country.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch yn fawr iawn. Again, the common ground that we have, and I also take a real positive from the fact that we have three party leaders now who say that they want to work positively and constructively. It won't be on everything—there are differences between us, we know that—but there's that positive sense here that there are elements of the work that we do in this place, from legislation to budgets and all sorts of other things, where we need to work together.

I must say that the accusation that somehow this is a rehash of our manifesto, that you have a manifesto, you stand in an election, you get elected, you have a mandate, and somehow then you tear up the manifesto and start again—. That's not how it works. That's not how it works. If this feels like our manifesto, as in if this feels like that it reflects what we promised the people of Wales that we would do, with the priorities on health and education and job creation and childcare and child poverty and standing up for Wales, it's doing its job, so thank you very much for confirming that, Darren.

You also criticise—. I get it; scrutiny includes criticism. I honestly say, on health, we face an uphill struggle because we inherit some serious issues, not all of which are the fault of the last Government, but that is what we inherited.

On PISA, don't criticise us on PISA scores. Those PISA tests were taken in 2025, before we came into power. But it does, of course, reflect again the scale of the challenge that we face.

The Member focuses, in particular, on health, and, yes, it is something that is important to me, but it's important to all of us here, I think, getting the NHS right. The Member's party has often made the case that we should declare a crisis. I do certainly believe that there's a crisis in many parts of the NHS. I'm not convinced that a declaration of crisis in that kind of way is particularly useful. There are suggestions there that we should have more about beds here. I have made the case for making sure that we maximise the capacity of our health system in the past, but it's not quite that simple either. Our surgical hubs—most of the people that will go through surgical hubs will be going home the same day. Also, in my local district general hospital, it's not a lack of beds; it's the lack of throughput and the number of people. It's the same wherever we are. The numbers of people who are medically fit for discharge and who are still in our hospitals, those are the issues. Should we have an ambition to absolutely grow where we can, including bed capacity, with the staff to go with them? Yes, absolutely. But we're also working within constraints. Remember that the plans that we have put in place and that are reflected in this document are clinically led, and they're not telling us what we need is more beds—they're saying we need a number of steps to be taken. But I'm not dismissing the point that the Member is making.

On the shift of resource towards primary—and I include preventative, I guess, in that, though preventative is a little bit different too—the Member's right that you have to be careful. We're not suggesting going in one leap. We're talking about 0.5 percentage point per year of an increase. But it happens in a slow and sustainable way because you don't want a detrimental impact on secondary care, which, in many ways, is the expensive end of the health service. And getting those waiting lists down, the higher waiting times in particular, takes then the pressure, hopefully, off secondary care, which helps then that transition to primary care.

The leader of the Conservative group says that there's a lot of ambition in this document that we share. That's good. So, let's work on those areas. The same invitation goes to Members in other parties. This is about ambition, as it says, but, at the end of the day, we're going to be measured on whether we are able to realise, if not 100 per cent, the thrust of what we say we're going to try to achieve on behalf of the people of Wales here.

Thank you for your statement, First Minister. It's great to see that raising standards in our schools continues to be one of this Government's key aspirations. And I believe that this was also clear from the statement made by the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language last week. The foundational literacy and numeracy plan offers a golden opportunity to get the infrastructure right. There's little doubt that the process of implementation and of delivering better results will be a major challenge. But, as the Cabinet Minister said last week, we must not apologise for setting our standards and our expectations high. There is a clear timetable for completing this task and it is an ambitious programme.

It comes at a time when schools are already dealing with increasingly complex pupil needs, concerns regarding student behaviour, teachers' workload, and challenges in recruiting and retaining staff. Bearing in mind the plan's importance and our aspirations for education, what further support will the Welsh Government be providing to teachers and to staff more broadly during this Senedd term in order to ensure that they receive the appropriate support to deliver this plan?

Diolch am y datganiad, Brif Weinidog. Mae'n wych gweld bod codi safonau yn ein hysgolion yn un o ddyheadau allweddol y Llywodraeth hon. Ac rwy'n credu bydd hynny hefyd yn amlwg o ddatganiad y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Addysg a'r Gymraeg yr wythnos diwethaf. Mae'r cynllun llythrennedd a rhifedd sylfaenol yn cynnig cyfle gwirioneddol i gael y seilwaith yn iawn. Heb os, bydd y broses o weithredu a chyflawni canlyniadau gwell yn y pen draw yn her enfawr. Ond, fel y dywedodd Gweinidog y Cabinet yr wythnos diwethaf, ni ddylem ymddiheuro am osod safonau a disgwyliadau uchel. Mae amserlen glir ar gyfer cyflawni'r gwaith ac mae'n rhaglen uchelgeisiol.

Mae'n dod ar adeg pan mae ysgolion eisoes yn delio ag anghenion disgyblion sy'n mynd yn fwyfwy cymhleth, pryderon ynghylch ymddygiad, llwyth gwaith athrawon, a heriau o ran recriwtio a chadw staff. O ystyried pwysigrwydd y cynllun a'n huchelgeisiau o ran addysg, pa gymorth pellach bydd Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei ddarparu i athrawon ac i staff ehangach yn ystod tymor y Senedd hon er mwyn sicrhau eu bod yn cael y gefnogaeth briodol i gyflawni'r cynllun?

contributions.text_english: Thank you very much for those comments and for that question. Yes, this is one of our key priorities. Standards in our schools aren't where, I think, all of us in this place can agree that they should be. The new literacy and numeracy framework, I think, will turn out to be something very valuable in taking a new view as to how we strengthen those fundamental skills. But the Member, Dirprwy Lywydd, refers to more than just what is taught in the classroom; it is about the support provided to staff too. We know that issues such as school attendance percentages and behaviour in schools are all part of the factors that create pressures on teaching staff. Those issues are very interconnected, and are often tied in to poverty and disadvantaged backgrounds and so on. But what we intend to do is to bring different agencies together—the schools, health and care services, youth services and so on—in a framework that's properly integrated in order to tackle these problems in a holistic manner, which is something that has, perhaps, been missing in the past.
contributions.text_original: Diolch yn fawr iawn am y sylwadau ac am y cwestiwn yna. Ydy, mae hwn yn un o'n prif flaenoriaethau ni. Dydy safonau ein hysgolion ni ddim lle, dwi'n meddwl, rydyn ni i gyd yn fan hyn yn cytuno y dylen nhw fod. Mae'r fframwaith llythrennedd a rhifedd, dwi'n meddwl, yn mynd i droi allan i fod yn rhywbeth gwerthfawr iawn o ran cymryd golwg o'r newydd ar sut rydyn ni'n mynd ati i gryfhau'r sgiliau sylfaenol yna. Ond mae'r Aelod, Ddirprwy Lywydd, yn cyfeirio at fwy na dim ond beth sy'n cael ei ddysgu yn y gwersi; mae o'n ymwneud â'r gefnogaeth sydd yn cael ei rhoi i staff. Rydyn ni'n gwybod bod materion fel canrannau mynychu ysgolion ac ymddygiad mewn ysgolion i gyd yn rhan o'r ffactorau sydd yn creu pwysau ar athrawon. Mae'r materion yna wedi'u clymu'n agos iawn â'i gilydd, ac yn aml iawn wedi clymu i mewn i dlodi a chefndiroedd difreintiedig ac ati. Ond beth rydyn ni'n bwriadu ei wneud ydy dod â'r gwahanol asiantaethau at ei gilydd, yn ysgolion, yn iechyd a gofal, yn wasanaethau ieuenctid ac ati, mewn fframwaith sydd wedi clymu at ei gilydd yn agos er mwyn mynd i'r afael â'r problemau yma mewn ffordd gyflawn, sy'n rhywbeth, o bosib, sydd wedi bod ar goll yn y gorffennol.

contributions.text_english: During the election campaign, the First Minister said that the election was not about independence and that it would not be a priority during this Senedd term. Then, last week, he signed a joint statement with Sinn Féin and the SNP saying that Westminster's time was at an end. And now, today, in the programme for government that was published, it lists in the section of devolved powers the desire to pursue the devolved power to hold an independence referendum in Wales. Given the First Minister's comments during the election and then his comments today about his determination for an honest politics, I'd like to ask: what's changed between now and then?
contributions.text_original: During the election campaign, the First Minister said that the election was not about independence and that it would not be a priority during this Senedd term. Then, last week, he signed a joint statement with Sinn Féin and the SNP saying that Westminster's time was at an end. And now, today, in the programme for government that was published, it lists in the section of devolved powers the desire to pursue the devolved power to hold an independence referendum in Wales. Given the First Minister's comments during the election and then his comments today about his determination for an honest politics, I'd like to ask: what's changed between now and then?

contributions.text_english:
Well, nothing's changed. I believe in Wales being able to pursue its future as a normal country. I believe in independence for Wales. I think everybody knows that. Our manifesto stated clearly that we believe that the shape of our constitutional future should be in the hands of the people of Wales. I mean, I think that's a fundamental right, and that is precisely what we're saying, in that we should be the ones, as a Senedd, calling it, as the people of Wales, asking for it, who are able to set the timetable for this. Yes, I did say that the last election wasn't about independence, and I think I have had lots of opportunities to explain what I meant by that.

There's no referendum being pushed for by this Government now, but we absolutely believe that the people of Wales should be allowed to decide. I will use the influence that I have, hopefully, as Wales's leader, to try to persuade people to think about the challenges, the opportunities and what we might be able to do in future that we aren't able to do now. These paths are challenging and full of opportunity at the same time. The Commission on the Constitutional Future of Wales isn't an independence commission. It is about, 'How do we arm ourselves to make us, as a nation, fit for the future?'

Now, Reform, we know—we've heard it again today from your leader, and again, you're being honest about this—don't believe in giving us any more powers. You think we should settle as we are. You think that we should, at best, put what we have in aspic and just hope that somehow, through our actions as Governments, that we can make things better. I just don't see it in that way. I think, where there are things that all the evidence points to it making sense for us to have control over—policing, where we pay for most of it directly in Wales now, but have no accountability for it; justice, so that we can serve people better in constituencies all across Wales; so that we can make decisions about our natural resources—I just think that's common sense.

What the commission does is provide us a platform through which you can say you don't want it to happen, and I can say, and others, 'Do you know what? We should look at this and see how we can deliver this.'

contributions.text_english: First Minister, it's encouraging to see the first visible signs that this Government has a programme at last. Many who read the statement by the First Minister will have smiled to see the claim that the Government made a good start during its first 100 days. For many across Wales, however, a series of reviews and a series of postponed decisions felt like anything but progress.
contributions.text_original: Brif Weinidog, mae'n galonogol gweld yr arwyddion gweladwy cyntaf bod gan y Llywodraeth hon raglen o'r diwedd. Bydd nifer a ddarllenodd gyflwyniad y Prif Weinidog wedi gwenu wrth weld yr honiad bod y Llywodraeth wedi cychwyn arni'n ddi-oed yn ystod eu 100 diwrnod cyntaf. I lawer ledled Cymru, fodd bynnag, roedd cyfres o adolygiadau a chyfres o benderfyniadau'n cael eu gohirio yn teimlo fel unrhyw beth ond hynny.

contributions.text_english:
More concerning, however, is the continued failure to prioritise funding to areas of genuine need. Many in Cardiff will have heard the Trefnydd's contemptuous dismissal of my question earlier today. We've heard claims from Plaid Cymru MSs in the past that the additional learning needs funding gap was less severe in Wales than elsewhere—comments that teaching unions quickly criticised as out of touch with the reality facing schools.

And last week, there was an appearance of going even further, with Government Ministers appearing to cast doubts on the future of Flying Start. Whether or not that suggestion proves accurate, it has caused significant concern among those people delivering and benefiting from the programme. Will the First Minister take the opportunity right now to provide clarity and guarantee that funding for Flying Start will continue, as well as the prioritisation of those most in need? Children in some of Wales's most deprived communities should not pay the price for the Government's failure to properly cost its election promises.

contributions.text_english:
To be open here, I was listening to the Trefnydd giving what the Member called a 'contemptuous' answer. What the Trefnydd said earlier was that she believed there was poverty in all parts of Wales that needed addressing. And I absolutely get—I absolutely get—the fact that the Member is standing up for the people of his constituency, as I would expect him to, but we have to, as a Government, recognise that we have urban poverty that we desperately need to get to grips with and we have rural poverty that we desperately need to get to grips with. In some instances, they're the same answers; in some instances, they're different answers. So, there's no contempt whatsoever there.

There's a specific question on Flying Start, and I have heard Labour Members raise questions about the future of Flying Start. We're somehow being accused of wanting to take money away from fighting child poverty when this is the party that has been criticised by his too often for wanting to spend too much on tackling child poverty through the childcare offer. This phase of the childcare offer is literally being delivered through Flying Start. This is building on what Flying Start has done. More families living in poverty, incidentally, are not in Flying Start areas than the ones that are in Flying Start areas. Both are really, really important. We want to help them all. I hope that's clear enough.

contributions.text_english:
I'm very proud to serve a diverse constituency in Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, with people coming from all walks of life. For the first time, many individuals and families placed their trust in Plaid Cymru, and they did this because they believe it will make a positive, tangible difference in their communities. I have spoken to many constituents over the last few months who are concerned about the rise in hate crimes, poverty, housing issues and other matters that negatively impact on their lives and the lives of their families.

If we are to be a truly ambitious nation, we must place social justice at the heart of our agenda. An unequal Wales will continue to leave people disenfranchised and left behind. A more equitable Wales, where people can receive different levels of support to achieve a fairer outcome, could accelerate our ambitions for a more equal nation. First Minister, people have different starting points in life and face different barriers, so how will the Welsh Government ensure that equality and equity are at the heart of delivering its programme for government?

contributions.text_english:
I'm grateful for the question and the sentiment, and I couldn't agree more. It was very humbling, back in May, to see different communities in their geographical location, in their diversity, turning to Plaid Cymru and putting their trust in us, and we have to repay that trust. That's what it's all about. On social justice, I say, 'Hear, hear.' I hope that speaking loud and clear from this programme for government is the sense that this is about equity, it is about fairness, it is about equal opportunity, it is about social justice. We don't want the national development agency to be there to make Wales rich for its own sake. We want it there to make us prosper in every sense, where everybody feels a part of a flourishing nation that I know we can be. The measures on education are very much geared to making sure that education opportunities are there for everybody.

The attack on universality that we had earlier today, our belief in universality and making sure that we bring all parents in to the support that can be given through childcare, whilst, at the same time, emphasising the need to tackle child poverty through the Cynnal payment, I think all of that reflects something that I'm very proud to stand by. We will be measured by the way that we adhere throughout to those values of ours and, yes, building a united, peaceful Wales that rejects division is something that means an awful lot to, I know, the benches that I sit on, but hopefully all of us here too.

contributions.text_english:
First Minister, you call tackling child poverty the defining mission of this Government, but a defining mission surely requires something to be defined. In July, when I challenged your Deputy First Minister over Cynnal, I said that what she presented was a plan to plan, not a plan. She told me that she was baffled by my question. Well, I have now read your programme for government, and the bafflement should be on your benches. Four years of Government, and on your defining mission, you promise to develop another plan that will then set the targets, benchmarks and milestones. Cynnal itself remains something you merely seek to pilot. This is not a four-year delivery programme; it is a promise to work out later what success should look like.

First Minister, your new ambition already resembles Swiss cheese: impressive packages, but full of holes and left to ferment, increasingly difficult to disguise. So, please answer the question your programme does not: by 2030, precisely what measurable reduction in child poverty will your Government deliver?

contributions.text_english:
I've heard a lot of this plan-for-a-plan business. Government works out solutions to the problems we face as a nation. That's what Government does. We have a manifesto that sets out things we have decided, and it's clear what we need to do because the evidence is there. There are things that we have done already. The rolling out of childcare has begun. It's not something that's going to happen in the future, it is happening already. The introduction of free school meals has already begun, and there has always been a phased approach to that. Our measures on health aren't being planned, they are being implemented right now. But at the same time, you use the tools at your disposal: you use the civil service, you use civic society in Wales. We come here in committees in the Senedd and recommendations will be made by the committees that you sit on for Government to do things that we haven't thought of doing yet. That is how it works. We always seek solutions to the problems that Wales has. If you thought fighting an election, 'There we are, we've done the thinking; let's just settle down and do it', that's not how it works.

On Cynnal, it's a really good example. We know what we're trying to do with Cynnal. There are practical difficulties with implementing it because we don't have the powers. Again, a good example of why we need the tools at our disposal. But we think we've found a way of doing it: we're going to pilot it. The working group has already met four times. It's not something that we're planning how we're going to address this. It is happening, guided by my Deputy First Minister. I'm not going to apologise for thinking out carefully how we make decisions that will improve the lives of people in Wales.

contributions.text_english: Thank you for the statement.
contributions.text_original: Diolch am y datganiad.

contributions.text_english:
I've got two issues, and I genuinely really want to understand this. You keep using the phrase, 'I want the people of Wales to decide their future' in relation to the issue around independence, and I really would like some clarity on that. What does that mean? How will you measure it? How will you make sure you know what the decision is by the people of Wales? And just to put on record, I'm anti-independence, but, absolutely, we need more powers here in the Senedd.

Secondly, on child poverty, you have my absolute support for all the measures on child poverty that you're introducing, and the universality of it. That is essential, for Cynnal and, obviously, the roll-out of universal free childcare as well. Just to put on record as well, it was me as a Liberal Democrat who made the deal with Labour for the 12.5 additional hours from Flying Start to be rolled out. That was a deal two years ago, and we want to see more. And I do want to just come back to your Deputy First Minister and myself. When we were previously on the back benches, we were like a stuck record, saying, 'Give us targets on child poverty, give us targets.' So, I'm really interested: what are your targets and when will we hear about them? Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch yn fawr. I remind the Member that she voted against a supplementary budget that was proposing to roll out matters like childcare that were really important to her.

On child poverty targets, this has been a major issue in that we had 27 years of Labour-led Governments that did have targets initially, then they withdrew them. We will bring targets. We are developing a strategy. One of the reasons that we have called for a strategy is that the sector—people working in this area—wants targets. I'd rather work out what targets are meaningful rather than pluck one from the air. The work is being done on that now. In early summer 2027, we will have that strategy, which must include targets. We need to know what we're aiming for.

On independence, I compare the situation in Wales to Ireland, where the Good Friday agreement specifically says that a referendum will be called—. I'm not interfering with what happens in Ireland; they can do what they want to do. But it specifically says when public opinion is clear that there is support for it, then you ask the question. In fact, the UK Prime Minister suggested in the House of Commons last week that the same should apply to Scotland too. It's opinion polling. It's sensing the view of the population. I want to influence people in a positive way, and you too, to engage positively with the possibilities that come from pursuing a particular kind of constitutional change.

But remember, we work with what we have now. We have real ambition for our nation. I want us to embrace all the possibilities of being a normal nation, but we're a Government that works right now with the powers that we have now, looking at the powers that we could have next, and next and next, because it's all about building a nation, which is something that all of us should be interested in.

contributions.text_english: First Minister, I welcome the programme for government, and particularly the work to embed public health and preventative health across Government. One of the ongoing challenges is that the benefits of having a preventative health programme are often delivered years after the investment is initially made, whilst the pressure on acute services is direct and immediate. In considering that, how will the Welsh Government ensure that preventative health programmes, be that in physical activity, healthy eating, the early years, or tackling health inequality, are safeguarded and prioritised when budgets are under such pressure? And what measures will you put in place to show that preventative health is steering budgetary decisions across Government? Thank you.
contributions.text_original: Brif Weinidog, rwy'n croesawu'r rhaglen lywodraethu, ac yn enwedig y gwaith i wreiddio iechyd cyhoeddus ac iechyd ataliol ar draws y Llywodraeth. Un o'r heriau parhaus yw bod manteision cael rhaglen iechyd ataliol yn aml yn cael eu gwireddu flynyddoedd ar ôl i'r buddsoddiad gael ei wneud, tra bod y pwysau ar wasanaethau acíwt yn rhai uniongyrchol ac ar unwaith. Wrth ystyried hynny, sut y bydd Llywodraeth Cymru yn sicrhau bod rhaglenni iechyd ataliol, boed hynny ym maes gweithgarwch corfforol, bwyd iach, y blynyddoedd cynnar, neu fynd i'r afael ag anghydraddoldebau iechyd, yn cael eu diogelu a'u blaenoriaethu pan fydd cyllidebau o dan gymaint o bwysau? contributions.text_english:
It's an important question, and an opportunity to explain what the thinking is behind this. We have, for the first time ever, a Minister responsible for preventative health. That in itself is an important step forward, because what we have now is a champion for preventative action who has been tasked by me to work across Government to focus on that preventative approach. That's a cross-governmental way of working, and I think that's the beginning of something very exciting. I've called it a preventative revolution.

How to fund that and budget for it reflects that it's a cross-governmental responsibility. We've talked about how we've been able to weigh up and balance that preventative spend, but the truth is that elements of everybody's budgets will be part of this. And yes, the envelope is very tight in financial terms, but in making decisions where there are two choices, we choose that preventative approach. We can then make progress in a positive manner, I believe, in terms of ensuring that housing is made healthier, that food choices are healthier through the food strategy, steps within the health service itself, and so on.

One final point that I would make is that there is a view very often that preventative measures, as the Member said, take years sometimes to feed through the system. That isn't always the case. It is possible to make changes within a relatively short period of time in terms of diet, which, for some people, can reverse type 2 diabetes, for example. So, the Government is looking at what can have that swifter impact, because it is possible, whilst also having to look at the longer term picture as well. But I think that there’s a fundamental change of approach here reflected throughout the programme for government.

Mae'n gwestiwn pwysig ac yn gyfle i egluro beth ydy'r meddwl tu ôl i hyn. Mae gennym ni, am y tro cyntaf erioed, Weinidog sydd yn gyfrifol am iechyd ataliol. Mae hynny ynddo'i hun yn gam pwysig ymlaen, achos beth sydd gennym ni rŵan ydy pencampwr dros weithredu yn ataliol sydd wedi cael ei gorchymyn gen i i fynd allan a dwyn pwysau ar bob un o'r Gweinidogion i weithio mewn ffordd ataliol, mewn ffordd drawslywodraethol go iawn o weithio. Dwi'n meddwl bod hynny ynddo'i hun yn ddechrau ar rywbeth cyffrous. Dwi wedi ei alw yn chwyldro ataliol.

Mae sut i gyllidebu ar gyfer hynny yn adlewyrchu'r ffaith ei fod o'n drawslywodraethol. Rydyn ni wedi sôn am sut rydyn ni'n gallu cloriannu'r holl arian ataliol at ei gilydd, ond y gwir amdani ydy bod elfennau o gyllidebau pawb yn rhan o hyn. Ac ydy, mae'r amlen yn dynn iawn yn ariannol, ond wrth wneud penderfyniadau lle mae yna ddau ddewis, rydyn ni'n dewis yr un sydd yn ataliol. Mae rhywun wedyn yn gallu symud ymlaen mewn ffordd bositif, dwi'n credu, o sicrhau bod tai yn cael eu gwneud yn fwy iach, bod dewisiadau bwyd yn fwy iach drwy'r strategaeth fwyd, camau o fewn y gwasanaeth iechyd ei hun, ac yn y blaen.

Un pwynt olaf y buaswn i'n ei wneud ydy bod yna farn yn aml iawn bod mesurau ataliol, fel y dywedodd yr Aelod, yn cymryd blynyddoedd weithiau i fwydo drwy'r system. Dydy hynny ddim bob amser yn wir. contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Llywydd. Today I'm updating Members on the Welsh Government's work to develop an ethical defence investment framework for Wales. This Government is committed to international solidarity, respect for human rights and the rule of international law. We are equally clear that democratic societies have a legitimate right to defend themselves and that the defence, security and resilience sectors play an important role in protecting the freedoms and values that we hold dear.

The world is becoming more uncertain. We are seeing ongoing conflict, including within Europe itself, as well as wider geopolitical instability and increased threats to national security. Wales has a significant aerospace, defence and security sector. The sector supports thousands of highly skilled jobs, sustains important supply chains and contributes to research, innovation and economic growth. Industries such as cyber security, semiconductors, aerospace and advanced manufacturing, autonomous systems and artificial intelligence are all part of the wider economic environment. Welsh businesses and workers should be able to benefit from investment, innovation and growth, including from the defence growth deal.
