Diolch, Lywydd. Heddiw rwy'n rhoi'r wybodaeth ddiweddaraf i'r Aelodau am waith Llywodraeth Cymru i ddatblygu fframwaith buddsoddi moesegol mewn amddiffyn i Gymru. Mae'r Llywodraeth hon wedi ymrwymo i drefn y gyfraith ryngwladol, i barchu hawliau dynol ac i gydsefyll gyda gwledydd eraill. Rydyn ni yr un mor bendant bod gan gymdeithasau democrataidd hawl gyfreithlon i amddiffyn eu hunain, a bod y sectorau amddiffyn, diogelwch a gwydnwch yn chwarae rhan bwysig wrth amddiffyn y rhyddid a'r gwerthoedd sy'n bwysig i ni.

Mae'r byd yn mynd yn fwy ansicr. Rydyn ni'n gweld gwrthdaro parhaus, gan gynnwys yn Ewrop ei hun, ansefydlogrwydd byd-eang ehangach, a mwy o fygythiadau i ddiogelwch cenedlaethol. Mae gan Gymru sector awyrofod, amddiffyn a diogelwch sylweddol. Mae'r sector yn cefnogi miloedd o swyddi medrus iawn, yn cynnal cadwyni cyflenwi pwysig ac yn cyfrannu at ymchwil, arloesi a thwf economaidd. Mae diwydiannau fel seiberddiogelwch, lled-ddargludyddion, gweithgynhyrchu uwch ac awyrofod, systemau awtonomaidd a deallusrwydd artiffisial i gyd yn rhan o'r amgylchedd economaidd ehangach. Dylai busnesau a gweithwyr o Gymru allu elwa ar fuddsoddiad, arloesi a thwf, gan gynnwys o'r fargen twf amddiffyn.

contributions.text_english:
However, public support for the sector cannot be unconditional. Where the Welsh Government provides support through grants, investment assistance, trade promotion or wider economic development activity, people in Wales rightly expect that support to reflect our values and responsibilities. It's important that we recognise legitimate ethical concerns while supporting a focus on high-quality jobs that the sector sustains in communities across all parts of Wales. It's therefore essential that Welsh Government support is guided by a clear and consistent ethical framework. While decisions on arms exports remain reserved to the UK Government, it is right that the Welsh Government is clear about the principles that guide our own engagement with the sector. We recognise the need for greater clarity in how these decisions are made. That is why we are developing an ethical defence investment framework for Wales.

The purpose of the framework is not to exclude the defence sector from engagement with the Welsh Government, nor to duplicate UK export controls or licensing arrangements. Rather, it is to provide a consistent basis for Welsh Government decision making where devolved support is being considered. In developing the framework, officials are engaging with stakeholders and learning from approaches being taken elsewhere in the UK. The framework will recognise the legitimate role of the defence sector in supporting national security, democratic resilience and economic prosperity, while ensuring Welsh Government decisions are informed by appropriate ethical considerations, including respect for human rights and international humanitarian law.

Our approach will be based on enhanced ethical due diligence. In practice, this means retaining the existing UK legal and regulatory framework while introducing additional ethical considerations to support Welsh Government decision making in the areas mentioned earlier. This will be a proportionate approach designed to provide greater transparency and assurance without creating unnecessary barriers for businesses operating responsibly, legally and in support of our economy and security. The framework will focus on activity taking place in Wales and on the specific projects, products, services or technologies seeking Welsh Government support. This will help ensure that decisions are informed by a clear understanding of the activity being supported, its intended purpose and, where appropriate, its known end users. 

We're also considering the introduction of a proportionate self-declaration process for businesses seeking particular forms of Welsh Government support. This will provide additional transparency and assurance while avoiding unnecessary burdens on businesses operating responsibly and within the law. This framework will also inform Welsh Government participation in defence-related trade missions, exhibitions and business-to-business events, helping ensure a consistent approach across relevant areas of activity. As part of this work, we will also consider how the framework can support innovation and dual-use technologies, recognising that many of the technologies driving economic growth, including cyber, artificial intelligence, semiconductors and advanced manufacturing, have both civilian and defence applications.

Given the significance of this work, and to ensure a consistent approach, I have asked that, where legally and practically possible, any decisions relating to new Welsh Government investment support for defence sector activity are not finalised until the framework is published and implementation arrangements have been fully considered. Should a decision on Welsh Government support be required before publication of the framework, it will be taken by the Prif Weinidog, taking account of relevant considerations. This is a temporary and precautionary measure to ensure that future decisions are considered against the framework from the outset. I want to be clear that this does not represent a withdrawal of support for the sector, nor does it affect existing contractual commitments or the day-to-day relationship between the Welsh Government and defence-related businesses operating in Wales. It does not prevent ongoing engagement, discussions, due diligence or exploratory work with businesses where no investment decision has been taken.

contributions.text_english:
Wales has a proud tradition of championing human rights, international solidarity and the rule of law. We recognise and value the contribution of the workers, businesses, researchers and apprentices across Wales whose skills, expertise and innovation strengthen our security, resilience and economic prosperity. We reject the false choice between ethical responsibility and economic opportunity. At a time of increasing threats to security in Wales and beyond, Wales can support a strong, innovative and responsible defence sector whilst remaining true to the values that define us as a nation. We can take a balanced and proportionate ethical approach that reflects those values, while continuing to support high-quality jobs, investment and innovation across Wales.

The framework we are developing will provide a clear and transparent basis for Welsh Government decision making. It will ensure that support for the sector is guided by consistent principles and informed by appropriate ethical considerations. Publication of the framework will provide greater certainty for businesses, investors, universities and workers across the sector, helping to give them a clear understanding of how the Welsh Government will engage with and support defence-related activity in the years ahead.

We don't want to delay or add uncertainty, and that's why I've asked officials to bring forward the final framework for publication this autumn. Given the pace of geopolitical and economic change, the framework will be formally reviewed after 12 months and kept under regular review thereafter to ensure it remains relevant, proportionate and effective. That is the balance that we are seeking to achieve, and I look forward to providing further updates to Members when the framework is published in due course.

Mae gan Gymru draddodiad balch o hyrwyddo hawliau dynol, undod rhyngwladol a rheolaeth y gyfraith. Rydym yn cydnabod ac yn gwerthfawrogi cyfraniad y gweithwyr, busnesau, ymchwilwyr a phrentisiaid ledled Cymru y mae eu sgiliau, eu harbenigedd a'u harloesedd yn cryfhau ein diogelwch, ein gwytnwch a'n ffyniant economaidd. Rydym yn gwrthod y dewis ffug rhwng cyfrifoldeb moesegol a chyfle economaidd. Ar adeg o fygythiadau cynyddol i ddiogelwch Cymru a thu hwnt, gall Cymru gefnogi sector amddiffyn cryf, arloesol a chyfrifol tra'n aros yn driw i'r gwerthoedd sy'n ein diffinio fel cenedl. Gallwn gymryd ymagwedd foesegol gytbwys a chymesur sy'n adlewyrchu'r gwerthoedd hynny, tra'n parhau i gefnogi swyddi, buddsoddiad ac arloesedd o ansawdd uchel ledled Cymru.

Bydd y fframwaith rydym ni'n ei ddatblygu yn darparu sylfaen glir a thryloyw i Lywodraeth Cymru allu gwneud penderfyniadau. Bydd yn sicrhau bod egwyddorion cyson yn arwain y gefnogaeth i'r sector a bod ystyriaethau moesegol priodol yn eu llywio. Bydd cyhoeddi'r fframwaith yn rhoi mwy o sicrwydd i fusnesau, buddsoddwyr, prifysgolion a gweithwyr ar draws y sector, gan eu helpu i ddeall yn glir sut y bydd Llywodraeth Cymru yn mynd i'r afael â gweithgarwch sy'n gysylltiedig ag amddiffyn ac yn ei gefnogi yn y blynyddoedd i ddod.

Dydyn ni ddim eisiau oedi nac ychwanegu ansicrwydd, a dyna pam rwyf wedi gofyn i swyddogion gyflwyno'r fframwaith terfynol i'w gyhoeddi yn ystod yr hydref hwn. O ystyried pa mor gyflym mae'r sefyllfa fyd-eang yn newid, bydd y fframwaith yn cael ei adolygu'n ffurfiol ar ôl 12 mis ac yn rheolaidd ar ôl hynny i wneud yn siŵr ei fod yn dal i fod yn berthnasol, yn gymesur ac yn effeithiol. Dyna'r cydbwysedd rydyn ni'n ceisio ei sicrhau, ac rwy'n edrych ymlaen at roi diweddariad i'r Aelodau pan fydd y fframwaith yn cael ei gyhoeddi cyn bo hir.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you for your statement, Minister. At a time of rising geopolitical tensions and a fragile economic outlook, we should not be placing political ideology ahead of Welsh security, Welsh jobs and Welsh investment. What we should be doing is everything possible to bring defence investment into Wales and secure the skilled, well-paid jobs that come with it. This is a sector that employs thousands of Welsh men and women and contributes £1.5 billion to the Welsh economy, and there could be so much more. My concern is that this framework risks doing precisely the opposite and rejecting those opportunities that are presented. It risks discouraging investment, creating uncertainty and giving defence companies another reason to take their investment elsewhere.

And as usual, it will be the Welsh people who pay the price. They will lose out on jobs, Welsh businesses will lose out on investment, and communities will lose out on the economic benefits that come with both. If we look at a case in Marshall Land Systems, they are moving into Merthyr, creating hundreds of jobs and supporting Welsh families. That's exactly the kind of investment that we should be fighting for. It's also a clear example of the positive impact that defence investment can have on a community, and yet it's exactly the kind of opportunity that this framework could put at risk, through uncertainty and additional barriers.

There's also a serious question about what you've told the Senedd. In your statement today, you said that interim decisions on defence will be taken by the First Minister. Yet, in an earlier statement, you said that all decisions would be deferred until the framework has been finalised, so we need clarity on this point. Because businesses considering investing millions of pounds into Wales deserve clarity from this Government. And let's be absolutely clear about what's being proposed here today. The United Kingdom already has a national system governing defence exports. Companies exporting controlled military and dual-use goods are already subject to the UK's strategic export control regime, with applications assessed against national criteria and strict ethical requirements. Yet, your Government now wants to introduce an additional test that defence companies elsewhere in the United Kingdom will not have to face, creating a distinct competitive barrier for those seeking to set up in Wales.

So, what exactly does this additional test achieve and what happens when a company fails it? Defence investment is not trapped within the border of Wales; companies can expand in England, Scotland or elsewhere with ease. Investment can move, and when investment moves, the jobs, the supply chain and everything else go with it. So, before you introduce this framework, what assessment have you carried out of the economic consequences for Wales? What assessment have you made of the jobs that could be lost as a result? And how can you seriously ask this Senedd to support a framework when you've not released the criteria by which companies will be judged? That appears to be becoming a pattern with this Government—big on announcements, but remarkably short on detail. So, Minister, what exactly are the criteria? What will cause a Welsh defence company to pass or fail this test? Who will make that decision, and on what basis will they make it?

There's another issue that simply cannot be ignored. Your party has a long record of opposition to significant parts of the defence sector. Now, your Deputy Minister, Mark Hooper, once said that attending an arms fair is indefensible. Your culture Minister described an arms fair as 'a contemptible event', yet thousands of Welsh men and women attend these events to support those industries every year. And Plaid Cymru has explicitly opposed the renewal of defence systems such as Trident in years past. Now, those aren't my words, those are the recorded positions of Members of your own party and your front bench. And now that same party is introducing a framework that could determine which defence companies receive Welsh Government support and investment. So, Welsh businesses are entitled to ask a very serious question: how can they have confidence that this will be an evidence-based framework, rather than an ideological test shaped by Plaid Cymru's long-standing hostility towards the defence industry?

Minister, national security is one of the first responsibilities of any Government, and securing good jobs, investment and prosperity for the people of Wales should be one of the first responsibilities of this Government. Neither should be sacrificed for ideology. So, we call upon you today, for the sake of the industry, to scrap this framework, remove the uncertainty, back Welsh worker, welcome defence investments into Wales. And we can all get on with the job we were elected to do, to grow the economy, put Welsh jobs, Welsh prosperity and our national security first. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
I thank the spokesperson for his contribution and his questions. First of all, I'd just like to point out that it is normal, given the specifics and nature of this sector; most democratic Governments around the world recognise that through having a specific legal and, often, ethical framework as well governing this sector. Scotland, the Scottish Government, has an ethical framework governing this sector. The Northern Irish Government has an ethical framework. Effectively, the UK Government has an ethical framework in its export arms licensing policy. So, what we are simply seeking to do is to bring the Welsh Government in line with all of those other responsible democratic Governments across the world that recognise, when it comes to this sector, because of its sensitive nature, you need to have a proper framework in place. Indeed, I have to say, the representatives of the defence sector that I've engaged with have indicated a willingness to engage positively with the development of this framework, because they regard themselves, as individual businesses and a sector, as being ethical. They see nothing to fear here, they want to engage with us in the process of its development. 

The framework is not finalised yet, so I can't give all the detail. I'm trying to update Members as much as I can through an interim written statement that I gave, through an oral statement, and I will return to the Senedd once we have the framework in place, because I think, in this area, because of the legitimate interest that Members have, it's important that you are involved at every stage in the development of the process. In terms of the interim decisions, in my interim written statement, I made it absolutely clear that we would defer where it was practically and legally possible, and I've reiterated that today in the statement that I've made.

I think it was a shock to both of us then. We were both looking at each other wondering what was going on. Llywydd, I really welcome the fact that we're having this debate and discussion, because the TUC congress just happened and there was a big debate about defence and the future of jobs versus, I guess, peace, security and resilience and so forth.

You've talked about what happens in Scotland and in Ireland. I guess my question is: have you talked to the UK Government to see whether what we're going to be producing here is going to be that much different to what they already have? What I'm really concerned about is that if the framework comes out in the autumn period, we then have a debate and discussion, I'm assuming, about what that framework then looks like, we have a back and forward—. In the meantime, there are contracts on the table, jobs coming to Wales. Could those defence companies, other manufacturers et cetera—AI you've mentioned—then say, 'Actually, you know what, this is taking way too long. We're going to go and have a chat with Stephen Kinnock, the Secretary of State for Wales'? And then, while you're trying to work through this new relationship with him as well, could we then end up in a position where we're going around the houses, everyone's looking at each other and somebody's looking for an answer?

For me, this is about the jobs that are already here, protecting those. I completely agree in terms of having an ethical framework, as a trade unionist. I get all of that, I totally understand that. But, for me, this is about the companies that we already have here. Wales has more than 200 companies serving aerospace, defence, more than 50 organisations in maintenance, let alone all the colleges and all of the training et cetera, and the really good apprenticeship jobs that are here as well.

You've talked about the global situation. You've talked about what is happening as far as NATO is concerned. Lots of discussions. Everyone talks about, 'How much money are we going to chuck in the pot? Why is this more important than actually building homes for people?' I don't think that it's one or the other. I totally appreciate and understand where you're trying to go with this. My biggest worry in and amongst all of this is that we slow things down. Because like you're saying—you're not saying that this is about telling people, 'Don't come and invest in Wales.' You're not saying that defence manufacturing jobs are something that your Government would be against. Although defence, I don't think, was mentioned in your programme for government. I don't think that word was there. So, I was a bit confused, really, because I was looking through it and I was like, 'The word isn't there.' Based on what you've said today, there seem to be a lot of contradictions.

So, for me, can you guarantee that, whatever you do, you'll do in social partnership, the trade unions will be fully involved and engaged, and that this is about job security in the wider sense as well? We're talking about good jobs across the whole of Wales.

I'm really grateful for those comments, questions and suggestions, and also the spirit in which they were made as well.

The last point that you were making—I think it’s absolutely important that we will involve trade union partners in the development of the framework. The defence sector, actually, is a highly unionised sector, and I think that ensuring that we have trade union and worker voice in the development of the framework—. And we have to be mindful, absolutely, of our responsibilities to the workforce in this sector. The defence sector and the related sectors employ, already, over 16,000. There's been substantial employment growth, even in the last 12 months, and these are, by and large, high-paid, higher than average, jobs in the advanced manufacturing sector, which is a sector that we want Wales to build even further on its strengths. We have a higher manufacturing base than other parts of the UK. We've managed to maintain that in the UK. We don't want to stay there. We want Wales to re-industrialise even further, and those advanced manufacturing skills are highly relevant to the context that we're describing here. And there are further opportunities that we want to explore.

In terms of timing—. And, yes, what we're trying to do with the framework is get the balance right between these two really important and legitimate aims of public policy and of society. We want to see the economy thrive and generate the high-paid jobs, good jobs, everywhere, to coin a phrase. We want that, and we want it to be done in a way that's consistent with our values. I think it's really important, not just in this context, but in every context. It's not business over here and ethics over there. Many successful businesses and founders will say, actually, the most successful businesses in the world are the ones that marry those two together, so that, actually, you're in a situation then where you can be proud to go to work. You can be proud of the work that you do. If you know the ethical framework is there for what you do, then that is the way to actually motivate, not just yourself, but the workforce et cetera, and the communities that depend on these businesses. That's true in every sector, and that's why, as I said, nobody that I've spoken to in the defence sector has said, 'We don't want an ethical framework.' Many of them said, 'Look, we want to behave in the most responsible way that we can, and we want to engage on that basis.'

The issue of timing—yes, I think that you're right. Obviously, we want, for the reasons that I think will be well understood as we're developing the framework, where we can, to defer decisions until after the framework has been published, and after you, as a Senedd, and civil society and everyone else, and the sector have been able to see it. We will. But, obviously, there may be some time-critical situations where it is not practically possible or legally possible for us to defer, and that's why I set out again in the statement today that there are exceptional circumstances that every Government has to allow some flexibility in relation to, and it's true in this case as well. But I've set out in this oral statement how we will deal with those, if they arise.

Thank you for the statement, but I have to say, I'm really disappointed. This is not an ethical defence framework. It is nothing more than an ideological blacklist that risks Welsh jobs, investment and national security. Defence and aerospace employ 16,000 people in Wales, they generate £3.7 billion in turnover and they contribute around £1.5 billion in gross value added. These are highly skilled, well-paid jobs supporting communities across Wales, and I thank each and every one of those working in our defence industry and, indeed, in our defence forces.

Yet, just when defence investment is increasing, this Plaid Government has ordered investment decisions involving the sector to now be put on hold. There has rarely been a more dangerous time to send such a hostile message. Russia is waging war in Europe, hostile states are targeting our infrastructure, NATO allies are strengthening their defences. It is almost, with making statements like this, that old saying, isn't it, 'Nero fiddles whilst Rome burns.'

Our freedom and democracy exist, Wales exists, because brave men and women, previously and now, in our British armed forces are willing to put their lives on the line to defend them. But courage alone is not enough. They need aircraft, they need vehicles, communication systems, protective equipment and ammunition. And we need those jobs for Welsh people here in Wales. If Members support our armed forces, they must also support the people who design and manufacture the equipment that they have to go to war with and fight with, that keeps them safe. There is nothing grubby or unethical about that work. It is honourable, and it is vital to our security.

Wales should be competing for a greater share of rising UK defence spend and encouraging responsible defence companies to invest here. Instead, this Government—Plaid Cymru Government—is creating uncertainty as businesses decide where to place new contracts and jobs. Mind you, that attitude is unsurprising from a party that has refused to commit an independent Wales to full NATO membership. Your hypocrisy—not yours personally, but your group, your Government—is breathtaking. Defence workers are treated as morally suspect while an Opera Cymru production is advertised as a 'celebration' of nationhood, honouring as three giants the men responsible for a terrorist attack on an RAF bombing school less than three years before the second world war. One of those, of course, was Plaid's then leader, Saunders Lewis. Plaid subsequently adopted neutrality in the war against Nazi Germany. Lewis used explicitly antisemitic language, and wrote that Hitler had 'fulfilled his promise' to remove Jewish financial power from German economic life.

Instead of subjecting the people who equip our armed forces to an 'ethical' test, Plaid Cymru should apply one to publicly supported arts organisations that celebrate or platform those who have committed or glorified violence against the British state, whether it is an opera hailing Saunders Lewis and his fellow arsonists as national heroes, or public funding connected with Green Man while the festival gave Kneecap a stage. And in its first week back, it is absolutely disgusting that this Plaid Cymru Government shared a platform with Sinn Féin leaders, despite that party's long association with the IRA's campaign of terrorism.

So, Minister, how many investment decisions have been suspended? How many jobs, do you believe, are at risk? I agree with you, Jason—not often, but today, on your comments today. Were employers and trade unions consulted? Will lawful Welsh firms be blacklisted simply because Plaid Cymru disapproves—and you do disapprove—of their industry?

An ethical defence policy distinguishes between aggressors and those who protect us from them. Wales should stand firmly with our armed forces, with the workers who equip them and with our NATO allies. We should also stand firmly with the ethical framework that the UK Government has in place. This framework should be withdrawn, and I will be more than happy to vote against this later today.

I'm always disappointed when you're disappointed, Janet, and there were so many strands to that, I could be tempted to disappear down a few rabbit holes. But, look, let me just say this: surely there should be some agreement between us that there should be an ethical framework for business in general that should be applied.

I'll give you an example: when the UN guiding principles on global business and human rights was agreed at the UN, who was the first Government in the world not just to endorse it, but actually to produce a national implementation plan that created an ethical framework for every sector of business? Well, I'll give you the answer: it was the UK Conservative Government in 2013. So, look, you can judge us on the framework when it's published, okay. I'm giving you an update on where we are in the process. So, by all means, hold us to account in terms of the content of that when that is ready. 

I think you do mischaracterise our position in so many different ways. I don't have time to respond to all of them. But I was absolutely clear in my statement that we're creating an ethical framework that we believe is a solid foundation for the sector because it gives transparency. There is nothing to fear here for the sector. It's not a prohibition of the defence sector. I recognised in my statement that there is an important and legitimate role for the defence sector in the defence of democracy, not least in the uncertain times that we're living in, but it needs to be done in an ethical way. And I would have hoped that that would have been the basis for consensus across the Chamber, because, ultimately, the way we defend democracy in all ways is ensuring that we can actually point to the values that we are, ultimately, trying to defend.

Whilst foreign affairs and arms export licences are reserved to Westminster, decisions about how Welsh public money is spent are made here in Cymru. Plaid Cymru demonstrated leadership, acting on a long legacy of peace, leading the Senedd's endorsement for ceasefire in Gaza in 2023, the first nation to do so. This small act led to huge hope for a nation who, I assure you, felt all hope was lost. Now, in Government, Plaid Cymru can go even further by showing leadership on international human rights law.

A freedom of information request by Amnesty International found that the previous Labour Welsh Government had given £500,000 to a company supplying military components to Israel, despite assurance otherwise from the then First Minister. This shows a clear need for accountability and a more responsible way of investing in our communities, so it's reassuring to hear that this Welsh Government is committed to taking a different approach, developing this defence ethical framework, which no previous administration has done, establishing a clear and ethical approach to defence and security in Wales grounded in human rights, international law and our commitment to peace.

Recognising the genocide in Gaza was a starting point, and concrete action is now what we need to follow. So, will the Minister please confirm what difference this ethical framework will make in the manufacture and export of arms in Wales, and what are the expectations on companies once that framework has been launched?

I'm grateful to the Member for her contribution and for reminding us, in the world that we live in, why this is so important, of course. When we have—. We have, in the case of Israel, of course, and in the case of Myanmar, two states where United Nations commissions have found that they have been guilty of being in breach of the genocide convention, the most serious and egregious breach of international humanitarian law that is imaginable.

The framework will help ensure, first of all, that our decisions as a Government—. Because the UN principles that I referred to place a responsibility on us, as a state actor, as a Government, to ensure that, in our engagement with business, we are doing so in a way that is consistent with those principles and with the wider framework of international humanitarian law. So it gives us the framework whereby we can hold ourselves accountable in relation to the decisions that we make, basing them, in an accountable and transparent way, on ethical principles, and in a consistent way.

In terms of companies themselves, as I said, the framework is still in development, but in essence, of course, we will expect the companies involved to confirm that their operations in Wales that we are supporting are in line with the framework that we have agreed. So, at both levels, it gives us that transparency, that consistency and that assurance that what we are doing is consistent with our values, which is what you would want in any context.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Lywydd. I must, firstly, declare an interest as a former Ministry of Defence supply chain specialist. Many Welsh defence companies operate several tiers down complex and dual-use supply chains and may have little control over or even knowledge of the eventual end use of the components they produce. I'm happy that you spoke about Ireland earlier. They've already been through something, and Invest NI has already recognised that neither it nor its client companies can fully track the final destination of goods once they enter into complex global supply chains. While military and dual-use exports are already subject to UK export control regimes, this new framework will add additional uncertainty and compliance costs to Welsh companies. How will the Minister ensure that Welsh companies are not expected to undertake due diligence that they cannot practically perform or duplicate functions already being carried out by the UK export control authorities?

While military and dual-use exports are already subject to UK export control regimes, this new framework will add additional uncertainty and compliance costs to Welsh companies. How will the Minister ensure that Welsh companies are not expected to undertake due diligence that they cannot practically perform or duplicate functions already being carried out by the UK export control authorities?

contributions.text_english: Thanks to the Member for his question and for the knowledge that he was able to bring to it. As I said, I think, in the statement, where possible we will seek to build on the existing UK framework, where that has a tier of knowledge and information that is relevant. I think it is fair to say, absolutely, that the global context in terms of supply chains is complex here. We have to be mindful of our ability to fully audit, and some of this will be context specific. So, in designing the framework, we will have to focus very much on the activity in Wales of the entities in question, being mindful of our own resources and the information available to us.

contributions.text_english: We'll now move on to our next item, a statement by the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability, an update on the deposit-return scheme. I call on the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability, Llyr Gruffydd.
contributions.text_original: Symudwn ymlaen i'r eitem nesaf, datganiad gan y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd, diweddariad ar y cynllun dychwelyd ernes. Galwaf ar y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd, Llyr Gruffydd.

contributions.text_english: Thank you very much, Dirprwy Lywydd. Today, I am very pleased to be able to update Members on Wales's deposit-return scheme. On 20 August, I announced the appointment of Exchange for Change as the deposit management organisation for us here in Wales. With this appointment, of course, we move one step closer to a system that will reduce litter, increase the collection of valuable materials, support reuse and also, of course, will help to deliver a cleaner and more circular Wales.
contributions.text_original: Diolch o galon, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Dwi'n falch iawn heddiw o fedru diweddaru Aelodau am y cynllun dychwelyd ernes yma yng Nghymru. Ar 20 Awst, fe gyhoeddais i benodiad Exchange for Change fel y sefydliad rheoli ernes inni yma yng Nghymru. Gyda’r penodiad hwn, wrth gwrs, rŷn ni'n symud gam yn nes at system a fydd yn lleihau sbwriel, yn cynyddu'r gwaith o gasglu deunyddiau gwerthfawr, yn cefnogi ailddefnyddio a hefyd, wrth gwrs, yn helpu i sicrhau Cymru lanach a mwy cylchol.

contributions.text_english:
Now, the appointment of Exchange for Change followed a robust process to identify an organisation capable of delivering the scheme here in Wales. As the deposit management organisation, Exchange for Change will now work with producers, retailers, local authorities and other stakeholders to establish the return network, collection and processing infrastructure, producer registration arrangements and operational arrangements and systems needed before launch. As a producer-led scheme, of course, they will now play a crucial role in delivering a DRS that works for Wales.

As Exchange for Change, of course, has previously been appointed to deliver the schemes in the other UK nations, it means now that we will have a common administrator across the UK. This provides the strongest possible foundation for interoperability between the UK schemes and for businesses operating across borders.

As Wales continues to lead the UK on recycling and resource efficiency, it remains vital that the introduction of the scheme delivers clear benefits in Wales whilst ensuring the scheme is interoperable, as I say, with other schemes across the UK.

contributions.text_english:
The scheme will include metal and plastic drinks containers from day 1. Glass containers will also be in scope from day 1, but reflecting our manifesto commitment, we will work closely with Exchange for Change, and the wider drinks industry, on a pragmatic approach to glass. This includes the four-year transition period, during which no deposit will apply and in which no DRS-specific labelling will be required, as well as the phased introduction of reuse.  

Working with Exchange for Change, our focus is now on the scheme’s implementation by October next year, and on supporting businesses, delivery partners and consumers to be ready for launch. In doing so, we will work to ensure Wales secures the benefits of the scheme, including reduced litter, the capture of high-quality materials for recycling back into the economy, and a clear pathway towards the roll-out of reuse. The coverage of all materials ensures that the scheme can tackle the litter seen on our streets and in our communities, of all drinks container types, from the outset. It also means that we can not only retain more valuable materials within the economy, but it also puts in place a pathway to the roll-out of reusable drinks containers, and the benefits the best schemes in the world are already delivering internationally.

Litter is not only a blight on our communities, it also imposes costs on local authorities, on taxpayers and on land managers as well. As DRS has been proven to do in other countries, by preventing litter and capturing drinks containers of all material types, it'll not only keep the materials from polluting the environment, or posing a hazard to people and wildlife, but it'll also reduce the burden of litter management and clean-up activities.

With Wales having experienced significant wildfire incidents this summer, as climate change increases, it is important as well to avoid preventable sources of ignition. With the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service having identified discarded glass bottles as one potential cause of wildfires—as sunlight passing through glass can, of course, focus heat onto dry vegetation and ignite fires—it is a reminder of the risks that littered glass in particular can present.

A successful deposit-return scheme will therefore help deliver cleaner communities and public spaces in our town centres, parks, beaches and countryside. As a Government, supporting businesses, particularly our small and medium-sized enterprises, to successfully transition and benefit from the scheme is a priority. We will therefore work with Exchange for Change to ensure that small and medium-sized businesses are fully engaged as we progress to implementation.

The success of the scheme depends on the participation of businesses of all sizes, and the regulations therefore include low-volume producer exemptions, exemptions as well for smaller retailers where that's appropriate, and flexible return arrangements. Together, these measures provide certainty and reduce compliance costs, and the four-year transition period, of course, for the deposit on glass also gives businesses more time to adapt.

Following on from the passing of the legislation by the Senedd earlier this year, the appointment of the deposit management organisation is a significant step forward to the delivery of DRS here in Wales.

contributions.text_english:
Maintaining current recycling performance is not the only aim of the scheme. It is also to capture valuable materials that would otherwise be littered, lost from the recycling system, or collected at a lower quality, whilst also laying the foundations for moving further up the waste hierarchy towards reuse.

I am confident, therefore, that by working collaboratively with, and in partnership with Exchange for Change, the deposit-return scheme will be successful in reducing litter, as I've said, but also in supporting the transition to reuse and reinforcing Wales's position as a global leader in resource efficiency. This, Dirprwy Lywydd, is an investment in cleaner communities, in a stronger circular economy, and in a more resilient Wales for future generations. Thank you.

Dwi’n hyderus drwy weithio gydag, ac mewn partneriaeth gydag Exchange for Change, y bydd y cynllun dychwelyd ernes yn llwyddiannus yn lleihau sbwriel, fel dwi'n dweud, ond hefyd yn cefnogi’r newid tuag at ailddefnyddio ac yn atgyfnerthu safle Cymru fel arweinydd byd eang ym maes effeithlonrwydd adnoddau. Mae hwn, Ddirprwy Lywydd, yn fuddsoddiad mewn cymunedau glanach, mewn economi gylchol gryfach ac mewn Cymru fwy cydnerth i genedlaethau’r dyfodol. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Minister, for your statement. We're clearly driving forward with the deposit-return scheme, but I simply don't think this Chamber or the general public, certainly Welsh families and Welsh businesses, truly understand what is coming next October, whether the scheme includes plastic, aluminium or glass containers. The fact that we're virtually empty here in the Chamber just shows that people don't understand it. So, I really thank you for allowing me to do this very briefly.

Let me begin. This is the current system of recycling in Wales. We have the highest recycling rates in Wales. Yes, shop, containers, home, Trolibocs, council, they sort it out, they make the money. Okay. This is what's going to happen now. We're going to go to the shop, we're going to buy containers, they're going to have a 20p flat rate on them, they're going to go to homes, and we've got to return them to retail. We've got to take them to these vending machines to get our 20 pences back. Meanwhile, the council have still got to pick up all the low-value recycling. Think about this here, I'm going to talk about this in a minute. Okay, that's the new system. I'll show you this outside if you want more detail.

Obviously, DRS was introduced by the Conservatives in the Environment Act 2021, and I do not understand—[Interruption.] I know, that's why I left. [Laughter.] We are going to have a second parallel system that requires people to drive, transport and return these containers separately. Why are we moving material around twice? Think of the emissions. Why are we building a system around thousands of reverse vending machines? The shops have got to buy these machines. We're locking ourselves into technology that belongs to the past. When you get to the machine and you put your bottle in, you get a paper ticket. It's not the 1980s. It's ridiculous.

And then there's the cost. This is the most serious point for me. Cost of living—every family in Wales is feeling the cost of living. Now we're being told that every drinks container will carry an extra charge. Say you're buying a 24-pack of water bottles, that's £4.80 to the bill upfront. Yes, we're told we can get it back, but we all know not every deposit will be redeemed. You'll lose your paper ticket. Some families just won't get round to doing it. And what about online food delivery? For people that don't want to or can't go to supermarkets—the elderly, the vulnerable, people with health conditions, disabilities—how do they get back their 20p? So, Minister, here's your first question: how will people that use online delivery and don't go to supermarkets get their 20p back?

And where does all this unredeemed money go? It goes into a private scheme administrator, sitting in a bank account earning lots of interest. A private, not-for-profit organisation, chief execs paid very nicely, and there's very little public understanding of who controls that money and how it will be spent. So, second question, Minister: how long will those unredeemed 20 pences be kept in that private bank account earning interest, and who decides how and when that money is spent?

Oh, perhaps the biggest issue of all is one that's not been discussed today at all in the statement: council revenues. This scheme quietly removes some of the most valuable recyclable materials, like aluminium, from local authority recycling streams—the materials that help councils generate revenue and offset collection costs. For years, councils have built recycling services around those materials, and now we're proposing to remove them and hand control elsewhere.

I've got letters and statements here from companies and member organisations in England—the Association of Directors of Environment, Economy, Planning and Transport and the National Association of Waste Disposal Officers—lots of different companies that recycle for local authorities, basically saying, and I quote from one of them, 'DRS would duplicate a system that is already costing local authorities hundreds of thousands of pounds each year', and they want it to be paused. This is in England. So, my third question to the Minister is: what impact assessments has the Welsh Government done on local council revenues in this new system?

Now, let's look at our friends in Ireland. They're about two years ahead of us. I noticed the statement said that it was working well in other countries. Well, I've spoken to our counterparts over the Irish sea. There are constant problems with the machines. They either break down or they fill up quickly. People hate them. It creates litter. Listen to this: Dublin City Council has spent hundreds of thousands of pounds—I think it's about £800,000—cleaning up after scavenging for bottles and cans from litter bins. They pull all the litter out, they find the valuable product, they don't put the litter back in.

Control, like the plan for Wales, is with a non-government organisation. That organisation now sits on €98 million of unredeemed deposits, because that's what happens when you devise a system that hasn't been thought through on the impact to everyday life, what we're asking people to do, to take their containers back to the vending machines. My goodness, there's enough to do in life already. And by removing those valuable recyclable products from household waste management in Ireland, bin collection charges—it’s a slightly different system to us here—have gone up by 30 per cent.

If litter was the issue, there are simpler and cheaper ways to tackle it. For me, I would scrap this scheme and we should be improving and modernising our world-leading kerbside recycling system. Part of the extended producer responsibility tax could be ring-fenced by UK Government with Barnett consequentials to invest in the latest technology, so these high-value materials can still be picked up kerbside, and we can start building processing plants here in Wales.

Minister, DRS is a reform too far. It will have a massive impact on Welsh recycling records, Welsh communities and Welsh pockets. Please: pause, wait.

contributions.text_english:
Well, what I would say initially is if we pause, if we wait, then I have no doubt that you would be on your feet then complaining about the risk of fraud. Because the rest of the UK is moving in this direction, okay? And everybody who was up in arms saying, 'Oh, if Wales isn’t moving in this direction then there will be fraud, there will be all sorts of problems and all sorts of concerns'—[Interruption.] The other parts of the UK would be the first to complain. So, we are all on a journey here, but what we have to recognise is that Wales is starting from a very different place.

We are asking producers, local authorities, consumers as well, to do something different. But if we are asking them to do something different, then we have to see a benefit from that, and including glass in the scheme is one benefit that we want to realise, because we need to keep that glass in the system. The one element that you have neglected, I think, in your analysis, is that this takes us closer to reuse. It's not about recycling. We need to move further up the waste hierarchy. Reuse would allow the same bottle to stay in use a number of times, reducing costs in terms of businesses that have to source those materials regularly. So, there are other benefits.

Littering, I mentioned in my statement. We have good records for recycling in the domestic space. We have regulations around improved recycling in business and in the workplace. On-the-go littering is a big problem, but this can be a big part of the answer, as we've seen from some of the international examples, where we can really bear down on on-the-go littering. A Keep Wales Tidy survey showed that drinks-related litter is on 43.6 per cent of our streets—nearly half of our streets are littered just by drinks-related litter. This can take us a step along that journey, reducing costs then, of course, for local authorities, for the work in terms of collecting some of that. And I mentioned the dangers from broken glass as well—well rehearsed. We know that there's more that we can and we need to do.

It's a deposit. It's a deposit; it's not an additional cost. Yes, those return points need to be accessible, of course they do, but there is no deposit payable in the first four years. This is a process of education, a process of working now with Exchange for Change to make those points as accessible and as easy to reach as possible. They won't only be in retail. I can imagine there'll be public spaces where those return points will be available as well. Where people tend to go or gather, we can provide them. And that as well is something that I think we need to keep in mind.

And council revenues, there are new waste streams coming online. Plastic film is one that's being trialled and developed now. There will be an additional stream of revenue coming for that. So, it's about striking that right balance.

The key thing for me coming from this statement today is that we now have a DMO here in Wales that brings us that partnership. That UK-wide partnership is embedded, really, because it's the same DMO that's delivering these services in all parts of the UK. And of course it's business led, it’s industry led; Exchange for Change is industry led. So, they can work with businesses, and we and others can make sure that we speak up for the communities as well in that process, as we work to delivering the operational model.

Some people want to scaremonger. There are legitimate issues that will need to be addressed over the next 12 months, but that's the point: we work up to October and the start date. I can't wait for us to get a point where, in five years' time, potentially, when the deposits kick in in terms of people paying, we will see a real material difference on the ground.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Minister, for your statement. I really welcome this update, building on the work of successive Welsh Governments. The appointment of a deposit management organisation for Wales is a vital step forward. Exchange for Change's new role as that common UK administrator makes sense in terms of joined-up working and providing clarity for businesses. I'd like to start by thanking everyone in Wales who recycles. It's due to them that Wales ranks so highly in terms of worldwide recycling rates.

It's important that businesses and consumers are given that feed-in. Secondly, the examples for low-volume producers and smaller retailers are important. I'd be grateful if you could set out a little more of the Welsh Government's current thinking around this. We know the key determinant of the scheme's viability is linked to things like how the scheme works, the level of fees or wider infrastructure, not necessarily just business size. So, what will constitute low volume and what will be done to ensure there are no unintended consequences?

This is my last question. Members may have seen the briefing produced by the last Senedd's cross-party group on littering, which was chaired by Mick Antoniw, on a deposit-return scheme. That document really powerfully makes the case that in addition to the scheme's immediate benefits for reducing litter, the greatest long-term carbon savings will come from well-designed reuse models built on that infrastructure—a once-in-a-generation opportunity indeed. Minister, you hinted at that and the importance of reuse in your statement, but could you say a little more about how this will be embedded across Government so we don't let this opportunity slip?

Thank you very much for welcoming this. Clearly, we're building on work that was done previously by our predecessor Government. It's something we inherited, but it's something we're embracing, and we're working hard to make sure that it works for everyone.

The biggest milestone is October next year, of course. That is when the scheme goes live across the UK. I know people have been concerned that we have been a little bit behind the curve in terms of appointing the DMO, so work is now happening on an official level to identify exactly how that is going to be achieved. I'm happy for a briefing to be held for Members—it's something I think we should do more of—just to sit down with Members, to respond to some of those concerns that some people are still raising, but also maybe to talk through the process in finer detail.

With the exemptions, you will be aware that some of the exemptions were outlined in regulations—from export shops to drinks supplied before the relevant commencement of the scheme. Small product lines are defined in the regulations, but also 'drink now' sales and hospitality. You will have situations where something is bought on premises, drunk on premises, so there are clear exemptions there. Again, I'm happy to write to you with that list in totality.

On the final point you made, the benefits of reuse are clear to us all. I touched earlier on the fact that it reduces costs in terms of having to source bottle after bottle and raw materials to produce those containers. But also there's a benefit in environmental terms in not having to keep creating those materials. But the quality of recycled material as well, when it is recycled, is much better, which, of course, is more valuable in terms of revenue streams. But keeping valuable resources like that in circulation for as long as possible is what we're trying to achieve here.

There are also additional economic benefits embedded in the whole process, because if we are reusing bottles, then we need reuse hubs, we need washeries, and those create jobs. I've seen a figure that a properly implemented DRS scheme would generate potentially up to 3,000 jobs across the UK. So, there are multiple benefits that we could realise here, but it is a transition. It's not going to happen overnight and neither should it, because things have to be introduced in a pragmatic and practical way. But that is the journey that we're on and one I'm determined to pursue.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Minister, for your statement this afternoon. We on these benches do not believe that glass should be included in this scheme. It has been a position we've taken for a long time and we just think it complicates the situation and adds confusion to it. One thing that has to be crystal clear about any recycling scheme is that people have to understand it and buy into it, and the more you can simplify it, surely the better that has to be.

As someone who used to come down the link road into Cardiff Bay and see the massive landfill site that is by Grangetown there, one can really appreciate the steps that have been taken in recent years to make recycling an integral part of what we now all do, and the industry that's been built up in recycling and reusing the products that we use in our everyday lives. That makes perfect sense, and it's something we should embrace. I commend the previous Government for what it did in getting the recycling rates up. But I fail to see why the Government wants to carry on penalising the hospitality sector and bringing glass within the orbit of this scheme that it's proposing. I know you touched on it in your response to the Labour spokesperson, but given that there was a 10-week delay in announcing the operator of the scheme, how are you going to catch up that 10 weeks, nearly three months, between now and next October, which is due to be the start date, to make sure that it does go live in October next year?

The other thing that is really important is providing clarity on how the interaction between DRS and EPR will work. An exemption from the EPR fees for glass containers in the scope of the DRS is an essential precursor to the inclusion of glass. Although the Welsh Government have committed to this, they are yet to determine how the exemption will work in practice. This is particularly challenging given the difficulty in tracking where the container will end up for sale at the point it is placed on the market, as well as the different ways the producer fees for DRS and EPR fees are calculated, by unit or by weight. So, can you offer some clarity on that point, please, Minister?

And then there's resolving the regulatory uncertainty of the reuse. The reuse targets included within the regulations for the DRS are not currently compatible with the United Kingdom Internal Market Act 2020, given that the exemption of this was not granted. How are you going to overcome that particular aspect? Because you need to be compliant with the UK Act, otherwise you're going to be in the same position as Scotland found itself in. And maintaining accountability for post-transition periods. The transition period for glass, were it a 0 per cent deposit, is applied and there are no additional labelling requirements, which will end in 2031. At this point, a number of issues will come to the fore, including how the return of glass containers is managed within hospitality, the risk of fraud, of glass containers sold in other parts of the United Kingdom being redeemed here in Wales, the additional cost incurred by producers for other rolled-out glass return points, and how the aforementioned reuse targets will work in practice. So, some clarity on that. While you've got the four-year grace period, I think it's really important that we understand how this will be implemented after that four-year period.

And there's the impact on hospitality, which is critical. We hear week in, week out people in this Chamber talking about the pressure in the hospitality sector in their own constituencies. We must ensure that pubs and bars and other hospitality venues are fully considered within the implementation plans, particularly given the cliff edge of 2031. The Welsh Government must address operational impact specific to hospitality businesses, which have not always been adequately reflected in the policy development to date. How are you taking the hospitality sector with you, Minister?

Thank you. There's quite a lot there. In terms of why include glass, given the costs involved and the implications for business, for local authorities and the changes in consumer behaviour that will be required, any scheme that we run in relation to DRS has to deliver meaningful additional benefits for Wales, rather than simply delivering what we already achieve. We need those tangible additional benefits, and without including glass, we don't see that, because we're recycling as we are—much of that is already happening—but we are going further because we do need to move in the direction of reuse, because that's what brings us greater prizes further down the line. 

You asked about the 10-week delay. There was a robust appointment process first of all—we needed to be confident that, in appointing Exchange for Change, it was the right decision. I am confident that that is the right decision. One benefit that that brings is that given that they are delivering similar schemes across other parts of the UK, they could hit the ground running. They're embedded in this sector; they understand what's needed. That, I think, will allow us to make sure that we can meet the October 2027 target in terms of going live.

On extended producer responsibility, including glass in DRS doesn't create an entirely new cost burden, because drinks producers using glass already meet producer responsibility obligations under the EPR scheme for packaging, meaning that many costs will transfer from EPR to the deposit-return scheme, rather than being an additional cost. Nation-specific reporting requirements are already in place under EPR, so it's not a new innovation when it comes to DRS as well.

You ask about UKIMA. I am confident that we are compliant with UKIMA. If you want to write to me with what you are suggesting, then I'll look at that, but I'm confident that we're not stepping outside the scope of that in what we intend to do. And there is a transition period. I won't repeat the point I made about the risk of fraud. The biggest risk of fraud is if there's no scheme here in Wales, and there will be.

As regards pubs and bars in the hospitality sector, I think I mentioned earlier that there are exemptions for 'drink on' sales in specified settings. Where deposit items are supplied for immediate consumption at mixed retail premises or on-sale premises such as hospitality, then there are flexibilities and exemptions there. So, again, it's something that we're mindful of, and as we develop the scheme, these are exactly the points that we need to be making sure that people understand.

Thank you to the Cabinet Minister for this update today. I'm really pleased to see Wales continuing to show ambition and lead the way with DRS. We know that at the heart of DRS is tackling litter that we see across the whole of Wales and our communities, improving recycling and protecting our natural environment.

I also welcome the approach that you've taken to the transition. We're asking businesses, local authorities and communities to make a real big change here, so it's right that we really give them the time and the support that they need to get this right. With Exchange for Change now appointed across the four nations, there's a real opportunity here, as you've said, to make the system work much more seamlessly across the whole of the UK.

My question is this: how will the Welsh Government work with the other nations to make sure that the schemes work well together across the UK, while ensuring Wales can still retain its environmental ambition, particularly around glass and reuse?

contributions.text_english:
Thank you. I can assure you that we will continue to work across the UK nations on this. Certainly, I know that a lot of work was done by my predecessor and the corresponding Ministers across the UK—that is continuing. Officials from all four nations are working closely, as are regulators. With the scheme administrator now, the DMO, we have that alignment, in that we have the same DMO delivering. I'm confident that we can work closely together on implementation and that that level of collaboration will continue as we move towards October next year and beyond.

It's important that we progress along the waste hierarchy. We do need to deliver significant improvements in the collection of high-quality materials for recycling and invest early. There are huge advantages to being an early mover in this space. Okay, internationally, there are examples of other countries that have already done this, but, within the UK, we in Wales could be reaping much of the economic benefits, particularly around glass, because I have no doubt that, ultimately, other parts of the UK will catch up with us, but we will have the infrastructure in place. We will have the washeries, the hubs in place to deal with much of this, and the infrastructure and the expertise as well in that space. So, I really see this not only as an environmental policy but also as a policy that will deliver multiple economic benefits as well, and that goes for good governance, I think, in that we're realising a number of benefits from one particular policy.

contributions.text_english: We will now move on to the final item on today's agenda, a statement by the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning, building safety programme update. I call on the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning, Siân Gwenllian.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much, Dirprwy Lywydd, and thank you for the opportunity to update Members on the building safety programme. I will talk about the steps that the Government is taking to protect leaseholders and to ensure that the homes covered by the programme are safe, and that those living in them are treated with the fairness and the dignity they deserve.

We know that there is a person, and often a whole family, behind every statistic. Leaseholders across Wales have faced years of uncertainty. Many have been unable to sell their homes. Many have seen mortgage offers being withdrawn, they've seen insurance premiums spiral, and they've had their life plans hampered or put on hold. This is the lived reality that has caused genuine hardship and profound stress for ordinary people who did nothing beyond buying a home in good faith.

I want to be really clear this afternoon: the progress in terms of the remediation work has not moved quickly enough. And I recognise the frustration and the hopelessness that this has caused to many. Leaseholders did not create this situation and they should not be made to bear its weight.

Their accounts have stayed with me, and they have shaped my determination to take action on their behalf. That is why I am pleased to announce today the launch of the Wales interim measures alarm grant. This grant will provide financial support to leaseholders who are facing the costs of interim alarm systems that are required to support a simultaneous evacuation policy. Further detail on eligibility and how people can access the support will be available shortly, and I will ensure that this information reaches the relevant people as quickly as possible. And I do hope that this announcement will make a meaningful difference to leaseholders who are shouldering the costs of interim measures.  

Turning to the Building Safety (Wales) Act 2026, I'm pleased to say that we are making steady progress with implementation. The Act marks a major step forward in delivering lasting building safety reform in Wales. The Act strengthens the regulatory framework for multi-occupied residential buildings and it introduces new competence requirements for fire risk assessors. The Act also creates stronger mechanisms to hold building owners to account, and it gives residents a stronger voice in matters affecting their safety.

Everyone knows what my view is now, which is that leaseholders should not be expected to pay for remediation costs that they did not cause. And I do believe that, wherever possible, the people who developed, commissioned or profited from unsafe buildings should be responsible. And that's why I worked hard to ensure that the Act did include provisions that allow interested parties to apply to the residential property tribunal for remediation orders and remediation contribution orders covering fire and structural safety defects.

The consultation on the regulations that are needed to support this element of the regime closed earlier this month, and I hope to the lay regulations before the Christmas recess. Over the coming year, we’ll continue consulting on the regulations that are required to underpin the wider regime as part of our planned implementation schedule. And we anticipate that the registration of category 1 buildings will begin in December 2027. I'll keep Members updated as the implementation programme progresses.

The Act complements the extensive programme of reform already delivered through the UK Building Safety Act 2022, as well as the subsequent secondary legislation, and that underpins the new building control regime that came into force in July. The new regime strengthens accountability for duty holders and it embeds the enhanced competence requirements for registered building inspectors and registered building control approvers. Amendments were also made to approved document B of the building regulations last year.

Members will be very well aware the Grenfell tower tragedy is the backdrop to our entire building safety programme. As we remember the 72 people who lost their lives, I would like to provide an update on the progress being made to implement the recommendations of the Grenfell tower inquiry. Over a quarter of the recommendations have now been implemented in Wales, and I expect that number to double by the end of the year. We are addressing many of the recommendations through the legislative changes I have already spoken about. Additionally, we've taken action to strengthen emergency preparedness and to embed the lessons from Grenfell across the system.

Finally, I'll return to our remediation programme. Last week, I met with developers who have signed up to the Welsh Government contract. That was the previous Government's contract. I emphasised that all obligations under the contract must be met or I will consider all appropriate enforcement avenues in relation to any failures. I am committed to accelerating the pace of remediation and to holding developers to account. I will continue to update colleagues as the programme progresses, and I welcome the scrutiny work from Members, which will help us to get this right for the people of Wales. Thank you.

Bydd rhagor o fanylion am gymhwysedd a sut y gall pobl gael gafael ar y cymorth ar gael yn fuan, ac mi fyddaf i'n sicrhau bod y wybodaeth hon yn cyrraedd y bobl berthnasol cyn gynted â phosibl. A dwi yn gobeithio y bydd y cyhoeddiad yma yn gwneud gwahaniaeth arwyddocaol i lesddeiliaid sy'n ysgwyddo costau mesurau interim.

Mae'r Ddeddf yn cryfhau'r fframwaith rheoleiddio ar gyfer adeiladau preswyl amlfeddiannaeth ac yn cyflwyno gofynion cymhwysedd newydd ar gyfer aseswyr risg tân. Mae'r Ddeddf hefyd yn creu mecanweithiau cadarnach i ddwyn perchnogion adeiladau i gyfrif, ac yn rhoi llais cryfach i drigolion mewn materion sy'n effeithio ar eu diogelwch.

Mae pawb yn gwybod beth ydy fy marn i erbyn hyn, sef na ddylid disgwyl i lesddeiliaid dalu am gostau cyweirio na wnaethon nhw eu hachosi. A dwi yn credu, lle bynnag y bo'n bosibl, mai'r bobl sydd wedi datblygu, comisiynu neu elwa ar adeiladau anniogel ddylai fod yn gyfrifol. Dyna pam y gwnes i weithio'n galed i sicrhau bod y Ddeddf yn cynnwys darpariaethau sy'n caniatáu i bartïon â diddordeb wneud cais i'r tribiwnlys eiddo preswyl am orchmynion cyweirio a gorchmynion cyfraniadau cyweirio sy'n ymdrin â diffygion diogelwch tân a strwythurol.

Daeth yr ymgynghoriad ar y rheoliadau sydd eu hangen i gynnal yr elfen hon o'r drefn i ben yn gynharach y mis yma, a dwi'n gobeithio gosod y rheoliadau cyn toriad y Nadolig. Dros y flwyddyn nesaf, mi fyddwn ni'n parhau i ymgynghori ar y rheoliadau sydd eu hangen i gynnal y drefn ehangach fel rhan o'n hamserlen weithredu arfaethedig. Ac rydyn ni'n rhagweld y bydd cofrestru adeiladau categori 1 yn dechrau ym mis Rhagfyr 2027. Mi fyddaf i'n diweddaru'r Aelodau wrth i'r rhaglen weithredu fynd yn ei blaen.

Mae'r Ddeddf yn ategu'r rhaglen ddiwygio helaeth sydd wedi'i chyflwyno'n barod drwy Ddeddf Diogelwch Adeiladau 2022 y Deyrnas Unedig, a'r is-ddeddfwriaeth ddilynol, a hynny'n sail i'r drefn reolaeth adeiladu newydd a ddaeth i rym ym mis Gorffennaf. Rydyn ni'n delio â llawer o'r argymhellion drwy'r newidiadau deddfwriaethol dwi eisoes wedi sôn amdanyn nhw. Yn ogystal, rydyn ni'n cymryd camau i wella parodrwydd ar gyfer argyfyngau ac ymgorffori gwersi Grenfell ar draws y system.

Yn olaf, fe wnaf i ddychwelyd at ein rhaglen gyweirio. Yr wythnos diwethaf, fe wnes i gyfarfod â datblygwyr sydd wedi llofnodi contract Llywodraeth Cymru. Y Llywodraeth flaenorol oedd hynny. Thank you to the Minister for her statement this afternoon. The Minister told this Chamber today that progress on the remediation has not moved quickly, and I totally agree with her statement on that, but her predecessor said much the same thing. What we've not heard, for nine years may I add, is a satisfactory explanation for why so little has actually been done. I also note that there is not a single remediation figure in today's statement. So, let me put some numbers alongside that statement. As of the summer this year, out of 161 private sector buildings that developers are responsible for, only four have been fully remediated, which is shocking. Seventy per cent have not even started work, though most, we are told, have plans in place. The Minister's predecessor described this as significant progress. Well, Minister, if that is how they describe significant progress, I would hate to see what failure looks like. If those numbers have improved, though, why aren't they included in today's statement?

What has happened over the years though? Well, social housing has been remediated using public money, up to 100 per cent of eligible costs, through the Welsh building safety fund. At Celestia in Cardiff Bay, the Welsh Government funded cladding replacement on the social housing block to the tune of nearly £2 million. The other seven blocks at Celestia, including private leaseholders, remain untouched. Same development, same defects, but years waiting. Let me be clear, I do not believe that taxpayers should be picking up more of the bill—exactly what you've said in your statement—for the private developers. Those who have built these unsafe homes and profited from them must pay to put them right. But that cannot become an excuse for private leaseholders to wait years longer than their neighbours in social housing. The Government found the urgency to fix the social side. It must now find the same urgency on the private side.

Plaid Cymru claim they stand for fairness, so I ask the Minister: does she accept that this two-tier approach, faster action for social housing and barely there action for the private leaseholders, has been a failure of fair treatment by the Welsh Government? Just take Meridian Quay in my constituency, for example. Phil Lake, a resident, took an insurance giant to the High Court on behalf of residents. Their claim was worth more than £25 million. Only now, seven years after Mr Lake stepped in, is remediation expected to start, and will be paid through the financial services compensation scheme, not by this Government.

Today, in your statement, you announced a Wales interim measures alarm grant. Any help for leaseholders is really welcome. But, in England, the funding for these alarms began in December 2020. Wales is almost six years behind. And we've been given no budget, no eligibility criteria and no opening date in this statement. So, will leaseholders who have already paid the price for alarms get anything back, because in my constituency, and I'm sure of many of us sitting here today, people are paying around £500 a month for these alarms, which is more than some people's mortgages?

I thank the Minister for her statement today. As she said, the origins of this work are following the dreadful events of 14 June 2017, when 72 people lost their lives in the fire at Grenfell Tower. Following the tragedy, the Welsh Labour Government set out to deliver a new building safety programme for the benefit of residents of shared buildings across Wales, regardless of building height or tenure. Change on this scale is complex and time-consuming and resulted in one of the largest Bills ever to be considered by this Senedd. I was very glad to be able to take the landmark Building Safety (Wales) Bill through the Senedd, and I'm grateful to the current Minister, and others in this Chamber, for their collaborative approach, which ensured that a whole series of complex amendments were unanimously agreed at Stage 3. This, Deputy Llywydd, was a Senedd first and demonstrated a desire to get this right.

The legislation that we passed here in Wales is far broader in its scope and ambition than the equivalent legislation in England. Three key principles are fundamental to the Act. First is safety. While we can never eliminate all risks, we can significantly enhance safety by identifying risks and ensuring that these risks are properly managed. The second principle is accountability. The Act ends any confusion about who is answerable for managing building safety risks. It ensures that those responsible for buildings are held to account in law for their safety. The third principle is residents' voice. Residents' experiences and concerns must be heard and addressed.

But passing the primary legislation is only the first step. Our focus must now be on ensuring that the Act is fully implemented, so it transforms safety in multi-occupied residential buildings across Wales. We now need to ensure that the Bill is practical and deliverable, and this means ensuring that regulations are clear and achievable. The Act will be determined by secondary regulations and statutory guidance, and how housing associations, building safety authorities and fire safety authorities are appropriately resourced to deliver their enhanced responsibilities.

So, what proactive steps is the Welsh Government taking to address the specialist workforce shortages ahead of the implementation? I know that Community Housing Cymru has been sharing with the Government feedback from their members across Wales. It's important that the Government listens and shares additional information that will be brought forward by regulations, so that housing associations can effectively prepare. Given the financial impact of compliance, how will the Welsh Government ensure that funding mechanisms support compliance and do not force housing associations to trade off the maintenance of existing homes against the delivery of urgently needed new affordable housing?

I'm very aware of the financial and well-being impact on people waiting for remediation. The Welsh Labour Government proactively supported residents by putting in place contracts with developers, and this Government must continue to do everything possible to remove barriers to progress.

I do welcome the alarm grant announced today, but people need to know urgently if they're eligible, how much this will be and how they can access it. When in Government, I set up the developers forum, which met regularly, and it's really good to hear that the Minister is continuing that work. I look forward to further updates on the pace of remediation, something that all of us in this Siambr want to see.

I'm really pleased that you're also continuing with the Members' briefing, the technical briefing, that I established. Those sessions, I think, are really important for Members to raise with your officials really local issues. That's something we can always get to grips with, and I hope officials can follow that progress as well. But I think it's really important for Members to understand the parts of the Welsh Government and the progress the Welsh Government is trying to make.

But much work remains to implement a new building safety regime across Wales. I said when the building safety Bill passed that I hoped the next Welsh Government would bring forward a remediation Bill to further support leaseholders. So, now, Cabinet Minister, that you're the Cabinet Minister, can you confirm whether your Government intends to bring forward a remediation Bill? Diolch.

So, now, Cabinet Minister, that you're the Cabinet Minister, can you confirm whether your Government intends to bring forward a remediation Bill? Diolch.
